eLife.title: Applying functional MRI analysis techniques to whole-brain calcium-imaging data to investigate structural and functional relationships in Drosophila melanogaster
eLife.abstract: Clarifying the relationship between structure and function is important for understanding the brain. In Drosophila melanogaster, FlyEM and FlyWire electron microscopy-based connectome data, and whole-brain calcium-imaging data are available. We applied pre-processing methods from functional magnetic resonance imaging to whole-brain calcium-imaging data and comprehensively investigated the optimal parameters. Then, we found that the FC–SC (functional and structural connectivity) correlation decreased linearly with region of interest count, and this trend was the same in flies and humans. We also developed a new, more robust method to quantify the degree of pre- and post-synaptic segregation, and investigated this in the fly whole-brain. This revealed that many neurons have unsegregated synapses. We extracted highly unsegregated synapses and compared them with random-extracted null SC matrices. Their FC–SC correlation was significantly higher, indicating that these synapses contribute to FC well. Conversely, highly segregated synapses showed significantly lower FC–SC correlation and contribute less to FC. Neurons with unsegregated synapses, like non-spiking neurons, are spread throughout the whole-brain, and they are thought to have a significant influence on FC.

eLife.title: Developmental bias explains the evolutionary trend towards simple leaf shapes
eLife.abstract: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

eLife.title: Nitric oxide feedback to ciliary photoreceptor cells gates a UV avoidance circuit
eLife.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is a key regulator of animal physiology. Here, we uncover a function for NO in the integration of UV exposure and the gating of a UV-avoidance circuit. We studied UV/violet avoidance mediated by brain ciliary photoreceptors (cPRCs) in larvae of the annelid Platynereis dumerilii. In the larva, NOS is expressed in interneurons (INNOS) postsynaptic to cPRCs. UV stimulation of cPRCs triggers INNOS activation and NO production. NO signals retrogradely to cPRCs to induce their sustained post-stimulus activation through an unconventional guanylate cyclase. This late activation drives ciliary beating through serotonergic ciliomotor neurons during UV avoidance. In NOS mutants, retrograde signalling, ciliary activation, and UV avoidance are defective. By mathematical modelling, we recapitulate phototransduction and circuit dynamics in wild-type and mutant larvae. Our results reveal how NO-mediated retrograde signalling gates a synaptic circuit and induces short-term memory of UV exposure to orchestrate light-avoidance behaviour.

eLife.title: Krüppel regulates cell cycle exit and limits adult neurogenesis of mushroom body neural progenitors in Drosophila
eLife.abstract: Neural progenitors typically exit the cell cycle during development, limiting adult neurogenesis. Here, we identify Krüppel (Kr) as a regulator of cell cycle exit and elimination of mushroom body neuroblasts (MBNBs) in Drosophila. Neuroblast (NB)-specific Kr RNAi and the Irregular facet (KrIf-1) mutation prolong MBNB lifespan and enable continued adult neurogenesis. Despite low post-embryonic expression, pupal stage-specific Kr depletion or misexpression causes MBNB retention, revealing a role distinct from its established embryonic function. Persistent MBNBs retain the early temporal factor IGF2 mRNA-binding protein (Imp) and fail to fully induce the late temporal factors Syncrip (Syp) and Eip93F (E93). Imp co-depletion suppresses MBNB retention following Kr depletion, identifying Imp as a key downstream effector. Krüppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1), a hormone-responsive transcription factor, functionally antagonises Kr by suppressing E93 expression. Kr-h1 knockdown partially rescues MBNB retention caused by Kr depletion, whereas its overexpression drives tumour-like NB overgrowth. Together, these findings identify Kr as a lineage-specific regulator coordinating the Imp/Syp transition and E93 expression to promote timely MBNB termination. This work reveals how temporal regulators control neural progenitor lifespan and restrict adult neurogenesis, linking intrinsic developmental programmes with hormone-responsive pathways in the Drosophila brain.

eLife.title: Selective suppression and biasing of chemokine receptors CCR9 and ACKR4 through targeting CCL25 with de novo miniproteins
eLife.abstract: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

Cell Host & Microbe.title: Vagus nerve stimulation ameliorates epilepsy via a gut microbiota-butyrate-vagal axis
authors: Long Zeng, Junjie Zou, Yuting Xu, Jingjing Kong, Qingshan Xiao, Zizhang Cheng, Minghan Xie, Yuhui Wan, Anbo Zhang, Yunhao Luo, Yuhan Huang, Yanjuan Ye, Jine Yuan, Shan Xue, Xizhong Zhou, Peihua Cao, Zhaohua Zhu, Tao Xie, Haitao Sun, Yanwu Guo
Cell Host & Microbe.abstract: Zeng et al. demonstrate that vagus nerve stimulation alleviates epilepsy by regulating gut microbiota and butyrate production and trafficking via the gut-brain axis. This study clarifies the microbiota-dependent mechanism of vagus nerve stimulation and informs therapeutic target exploration for epilepsy.

Cell Host & Microbe.title: Drought tolerance-enhancing fungal pathogens reprogram plant cell identity through mRNA turnover
authors: Konrad Subieta, Leonie Weber, Jan-Niclas Lübbers, Toshihiro Arae, Karin Wiesotzki, Leon Pierdzig, Corinna Thurow, Johanna Schmitz, Ulrike Lipka, Ya Ma, Kai Heimel, Kerstin Schmitt, Andrea Thürmer, Anja Poehlein, Akira Iwase, Keiko Sugimoto, Rolf Daniel, Jan de Vries, Oliver Valerius, Gerhard H. Braus, Andrea Polle, Christiane Gatz, Misato Ohtani, Thomas Teichmann, Volker Lipka
Cell Host & Microbe.abstract: Subieta et al. find that the fungal pathogen Verticillium deploys the effector TRADE to reprogram plant cell identity. By targeting the mRNA turnover factor VARICOSE and promoting its phosphorylation, TRADE stabilizes transcripts regulating vascular differentiation, triggering the conversion of differentiated plant cells into water-conducting xylem elements.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Genomic analysis of Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolates reveals rare hypervirulence, no convergence with antimicrobial resistance, and a bla(SHV) promoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs at a German university hospital.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) and the convergence of hypervirulence with antimicrobial resistance have raised concern worldwide, but contemporary, prospective data from Central Europe remain limited. We characterized K. pneumoniae bloodstream isolates from a German university hospital, focusing on hypervirulence and antimicrobial resistance. Bloodstream isolates were collected at University Medical Center of Schleswig-Holstein, Lübeck, Germany, between May and December 2023. In total, 74 K. pneumoniae were genotyped using whole-genome sequencing. Genomic virulence and resistance determinants were characterized with Kleborate and Russo criterion. A core-genome phylogeny was reconstructed. Hypervirulence was assessed genotypically and phenotypically using string test, in vitro growth kinetics, and the Galleria mellonella killing assay. Findings were compared against 5,514 publicly available bloodstream-derived genomes. Genomically predicted hvKp were rare (2/74 by Kleborate; 1/74 by Russo) and belonged to the classical high-risk clones ST23 and ST380, neither of which carried acquired resistance genes. Eleven isolates were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins (nine blaCTX-M-15, two blaCTX-M-14), and two were carbapenem-resistant through blaOXA-48. Three isolates carried a C-112A blaSHV promoter mutation associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs (0.5-4 mg/L). Neither growth kinetics nor G. mellonella killing distinguished the two hypervirulent isolates from non-hypervirulent. In the public data set, the overall hvKp prevalence was low, with no significant increase between 2012 and 2025. In this cohort, hypervirulent K. pneumoniae was rare and showed no convergence with acquired resistance. These findings suggest that convergent MDR-hvKp lineages remain uncommon and support the continued use of genomic surveillance to detect their possible future emergence. [IMPORTANCE] Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKp) has emerged as a major public health concern because it causes more invasive and often more severe infections than classical K. pneumoniae, and its convergence with antimicrobial resistance could further limit treatment options. However, prospective data on the prevalence of hvKp specifically from bloodstream infections remain scarce, particularly in Europe. By combining genomic analysis of a prospective bloodstream-infection cohort with more than 5,500 publicly available genomes, we show that hypervirulent strains remain uncommon and that convergence with acquired antimicrobial resistance is still rare in this setting. These findings provide an important baseline for ongoing genomic surveillance of hvKp. In addition, the same surveillance approach also flagged a previously reported blaSHV promoter variant associated with elevated cefiderocol MICs, indicating a potential emerging mechanism that warrants further investigation as cefiderocol use becomes more widespread.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: RpiRA integrates effector maturation and cytolysin expression in Staphylococcus aureus.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Staphylococcus aureus is a major opportunistic pathogen whose virulence is governed by complex regulatory networks. Although RpiR-family transcription factors modulate pathogenicity in diverse bacteria, the function of the S. aureus RpiRA remains unclear. Here, we investigate the role of RpiRA in S. aureus virulence through complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches. Deletion of rpiRA did not affect bacterial growth but significantly attenuated virulence in a mouse subcutaneous infection model. Mechanistically, RpiRA directly binds to the promoter of the foldase chaperone gene prsA and activates its transcription. Loss of rpiRA also increased hemolytic activity, and transcriptomic profiling identified the psmβ operon, encoding PSMβ peptides (phenol-soluble modulins), as a direct target repressed by RpiRA. Notably, deletion of psmβ resulted in enlarged abscesses without increasing bacterial burden in vivo. Together, these results identify RpiRA as a key transcriptional regulator of S. aureus virulence that activates prsA and represses psmβ to modulate hemolysis and lesion pathology during skin infection. Our findings expand the known functional repertoire of RpiR-family proteins and provide new molecular insights into S. aureus pathogenesis. [IMPORTANCE] Staphylococcus aureus commonly lives harmlessly on the human body but can also cause serious skin infections. To cause disease, this bacterium must coordinate the production of damaging factors with their proper maturation and release. We studied RpiRA, a poorly understood bacterial regulatory protein, and found that removing RpiRA weakened skin infection in mice without impairing bacterial growth. RpiRA controls two linked processes: it activates a gene needed for the maturation of secreted virulence factors and represses a gene cluster that produces peptides involved in red blood cell lysis and lesion outcome. This dual regulation helps explain why stronger hemolysis in laboratory assays does not necessarily lead to more severe infection in animals. Our work identifies RpiRA as a new regulator of S. aureus pathogenicity and reveals how this pathogen coordinates different virulence outputs during skin infection.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: First report of the emergence of duck hepatitis virus 1 associated with duck viral hepatitis in young ducklings in Bangladesh.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Duck hepatitis virus (DHV) is the etiological agent of duck viral hepatitis (DVH), a highly contagious disease associated with significant mortality in ducklings. This study aimed to detect and molecularly characterize DHV in young ducklings from the Netrokona and Kishoreganj districts of Bangladesh between February and May 2025. Thirty-five liver tissue samples were collected from ducklings suspected of DVH based on clinical history, observed symptoms, and post-mortem lesions. Samples underwent histopathological examination and RNA extraction, followed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). For further confirmation, partial sequencing of the 5'-UTR of a DHV-1-positive isolate was performed, and evolutionary relationships were evaluated through phylogenetic analysis and BLAST search using the NCBI GenBank database. Clinically, affected ducklings exhibited angular arch posture, with mortality rates ranging from 35% to 80% among 4- to 10-day-old birds. Post-mortem examination revealed enlarged, yellowish-brown livers with ecchymotic or pinpoint hemorrhages. Histopathology demonstrated hepatocellular necrosis, hemorrhage, and congestion of the central and portal veins and sinusoids, accompanied by severe inflammatory infiltration. RT-PCR identified DHV-1 in 8 (23%) samples. Phylogenetic and BLAST analyses demonstrated a close relationship (97.26%-98.28% identity) between Bangladeshi isolates and DHV-1 isolates from India, China, and Taiwan. To our knowledge, this is the first study in Bangladesh to confirm DHV-1 infection as the cause of DVH in young ducklings, emphasizing the urgent need for vaccination to prevent DHV-1-related mortality.IMPORTANCEOutbreaks of duck viral hepatitis (DVH) have been reported around the globe. In Bangladesh, although duck farmers and veterinarians often complained of deaths in ducklings showing symptoms consistent with DVH, no documented studies have previously confirmed Duck hepatitis virus (DHV) infection. Furthermore, there has been little formal reporting of duck diseases prevalent in the haor regions of Bangladesh, and the causes of much of the mortality from economically important duck diseases remain undetermined. These observations underscore the need for research to clarify the association between DHV-1 infection and DVH in Bangladeshi ducklings. Therefore, this study was conducted to investigate DVH outbreaks among ducklings in the Netrokona and Kishoreganj districts of Bangladesh.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Humoral immunity to invasive meningococci following natural exposure and vaccination: insights into the MenW cc11 outbreak in the Netherlands.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Neisseria meningitidis colonization can result in invasive meningococcal disease. Following a meningococcus C outbreak in 2001-2002 and a subsequent MenC vaccination campaign, a MenW outbreak occurred in the Netherlands in 2017-2018, mostly caused by the same clonal complex 11 (cc11) as the earlier MenC outbreak. We investigated how meningococcal lineage and differences in humoral immunity to invasive MenC and MenW isolates may explain the MenW outbreak. Using rabbit serum bactericidal antibody assays (rSBAs), we assessed the serological protection against invasive meningococcal isolates (n = 56) from the Netherlands (2001-2018), representing diverse serogroups and clonal complexes, using pooled serum from unvaccinated or vaccinated individuals. Prior to the MenW outbreak, a serum pool from unvaccinated individuals showed limited bactericidal activity against MenW strains, but higher activity against MenC strains. In serum from unvaccinated individuals, increased binding of immunoglobulin (Ig) A and IgM to unencapsulated, compared to encapsulated, strains was observed. After vaccination, capsule-specific antibodies increased, accompanied by enhanced antibody binding to encapsulated strains. Pooled serum from MenACWY-vaccinated individuals demonstrated bactericidal activity against all invasive isolates. However, sera from some individuals failed to kill MenC and especially MenW strains. In addition, sera from vaccinated adolescents showed higher SBA titers than those from vaccinated older adults. Our findings suggest that the 2017-2018 MenW cc11 outbreak in the Netherlands resulted from a combination of low naturally acquired population immunity to MenW and enhanced virulence of cc11 strains. Continuous surveillance of meningococcal epidemiology and population immunity remains essential to inform vaccine strategies and prevent future outbreaks. [IMPORTANCE] The underlying cause of meningococcal outbreaks is only partly understood. Following a meningococcal C (MenC) outbreak of clonal type cc11, the same clonal complex was a major cause of a subsequent MenW outbreak in the Netherlands and other countries. We investigated natural and vaccine-induced immunity to invasive meningococcal isolates. Preceding the MenW outbreak, natural immunity in the population was lower to clinical MenW isolates compared with clinical MenC isolates of the previous outbreak. Natural immunity to these bacteria was mainly targeting membrane proteins with limited reactivity to the capsule in unvaccinated individuals. These data indicate that following meningococcal outbreaks, population immunity improves but is insufficient to prevent outbreaks by different meningococcal lineages. MenACWY vaccine-induced antibodies were bactericidal to all isolates tested, confirming the effectiveness of the vaccine to protect the population.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Repeated Treponema pallidum exposure induces a tolerized macrophage phenotype via HO-1-mediated suppression of NF-κB signaling.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, establishes lifelong chronic infection through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. A key feature is the establishment of a latent stage characterized by minimal inflammation despite persistent pathogen presence, suggesting active modulation of host immunity. Macrophages can adopt a tolerance state during persistent infections, but whether T. pallidum exploits this mechanism remains unknown. This study aimed to determine whether T. pallidum induces a state of macrophage tolerance to facilitate persistent infection. The induction and mechanism of a tolerant macrophage state were investigated using in vitro repeated-stimulation and in vivo rabbit infection models, assessed by cytokine profiling and phagocytosis. Prior exposure to T. pallidum induced a tolerized phenotype, characterized by suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokine (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-18) production, enhanced anti-inflammatory output (IL-10, IL1RN), and impaired phagocytosis. A tolerized macrophage phenotype was also confirmed in macrophages from chronically infected rabbits. Transcriptomic analysis identified downregulation of NF-κB signaling and upregulation of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) in tolerant macrophages. Inhibition of HO-1 restored NF-κB activation, pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and phagocytic function. T. pallidum induces macrophage tolerance by activating HO-1 to inhibit NF-κB signaling. This mechanism suppresses inflammation and phagocytosis, creating an immunosuppressive niche that promotes pathogen persistence. This finding reveals a key immunomodulatory pathway that suppresses host defenses, explaining how T. pallidum achieves persistent infection and advancing the mechanistic understanding of syphilis. [IMPORTANCE] Syphilis can persist for prolonged periods despite limited overt inflammation, but the mechanisms by which T. pallidum reshapes host immune responses remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that prior exposure to T. pallidum causes macrophages to become less responsive to subsequent stimulation, with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production and phagocytic capacity. A similar tolerant phenotype was also observed in macrophages derived from infected rabbits. Mechanistically, this altered response was associated with increased HO-1 expression and suppression of NF-κB inflammatory signaling, while inhibition of HO-1 partially restored macrophage responsiveness. These findings identify an important regulatory mechanism underlying T. pallidum-induced macrophage tolerance and provide new insight into how altered macrophage responses may contribute to the low-inflammatory environment associated with persistent syphilis.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Haloalkalitolerant Billgrantia alkalidenitrificans sp. nov. isolated from cathodic biofilm enriched with Soda Lake sediments and genomic insights into the key metabolic functionality of the Billgrantia genus.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Extreme environments host diverse but underexplored microbial communities. Many microbes remain uncultured due to the limitations of existing isolation techniques. This study reports a novel haloalkalitolerant nitrate-reducing, Gram-negative bacterium, Billgrantia alkalidenitrificans NRB1, isolated from the cathodic biofilm enriched electrochemically using sub-surface sediments from Lonar Lake (Soda Lake, India), and presents a genome-based analysis of the major metabolic functions of the genus Billgrantia, recently reclassified from the genus Halomonas. Physiological experiments demonstrated that NRB1 is a facultative anaerobe that displays remarkable adaptability to a wide range of salinities (0-150 g NaCl/L; optimum 20-50 g NaCl/L), temperatures (10°C-45°C; optimum 37°C), and pH (6.5-11.5; optimum 9.5). It is capable of utilizing several sugars, sulfide oxidation, and respiration on oxygen, nitrate (via denitrification), and nitrite. These experimental observations were consistent with genome analysis, which predicted a complete set of genes for denitrification, sulfide oxidation, and sugar metabolism pathways, also detected in other Billgrantia species. Genome analysis further predicted the presence of arsenic resistance and ectoine-synthesizing genes in NRB1. Phylogenetic analysis using the 16S rRNA gene, orthologous genes, and whole-genome sequencing revealed that strain NRB1 clustered closely with Billgrantia campisalis 4A, the closest reference taxon. Genome-to-genome distance, average nucleotide identity, and average amino acid identity between NRB1 and the closest reference taxa were lower than the threshold values required for demarcation of a novel species. This study also contributes to the limited knowledge of extremophiles and proposes a phylogenomic-based reclassification of Halomonas alkalisoli within the genus Billgrantia as Billgrantia alkalisoli comb. nov., while also providing genome-based insights into the ecologically relevant, diverse metabolic capabilities of different Billgrantia species.IMPORTANCEThe Halomonadaceae family comprises one of the largest and most diverse bacterial groups in saline/haloalkaline environments. Recent revisions of the Halomonas genus have uncovered substantial phylogenetic diversity and broad ecological distribution. This study presents a genome-based analysis of the recently delineated genus Billgrantia, derived from Halomonas, and describes a novel haloalkalitolerant species, Billgrantia alkalidenitrificans, isolated from a cathodic biofilm enriched using Lonar Lake sediments. This is a unique haloalkaline meteorite impact lake that serves as an interesting ecosystem for studying microbial adaptation, nutrient cycling, and extremophiles, relevant to astrobiology. Electrochemical microbial cultivation offers an effective strategy for accessing microorganisms that are otherwise difficult to culture using conventional approaches. By integrating ecological context, genome-based taxonomy, and comparative genomics, this work expands understanding of the metabolic versatility, ecological significance, and evolutionary coherence of the genus Billgrantia, emphasizing its importance in haloalkaline ecosystems and its relevance to element cycling and bioelectrochemical technologies.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: cp BVDV NADL infection remodels MAMs and alters IP3R associated ER-mitochondrial signaling.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membranes (MAMs) are important interorganelle contact regions that coordinate Ca²+ signaling, cellular metabolism, and apoptosis. Cytopathic (cp) bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) causes pronounced cytopathic effects; however, whether it promotes viral replication by remodeling host organelle interactions and MAMs remains unclear. The results showed that cp BVDV NADL infection induced ER stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis, as evidenced by reduced OXPHOS related protein levels, mitochondrial ROS accumulation, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, an increased relative Rhod-2 detectable mitochondrial Ca²⁺ signal, enhanced mPTP opening, and cytosolic cytochrome c accumulation. Treatment with 4-PBA significantly alleviated mitochondrial dysfunction and inhibited BVDV replication. Further investigation revealed that cp BVDV NADL infection shortened the mean ER-mitochondrial intermembrane distance and was accompanied by reduced IP3R protein levels. The results also suggested that lysosome and proteasome associated degradation pathways may contribute to IP3R protein downregulation. In contrast, neither ncp BVDV NY-1 nor UV inactivated cp BVDV NADL significantly reduced IP3R protein levels. In addition, saRNA mediated IP3R upregulation improved mitochondrial function, reduced apoptosis, and inhibited viral replication. Co-IP, supported by the overlapping subcellular distributions observed by immunofluorescence, suggested a possible association between NS4B and IP3R. These findings indicate that replication competent cp BVDV NADL induces structural and functional remodeling of MAMs, accompanied by dysregulated IP3R regulation, disrupted mitochondrial Ca²⁺ homeostasis, and organelle dysfunction. These alterations are associated with enhanced viral replication and may provide potential targets for intervention against BVDV infection. [IMPORTANCE] Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) causes substantial economic losses to the cattle industry, yet how it affects host organelle communication during infection remains unclear. This study shows that replication-competent cytopathic BVDV NADL remodels mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membranes (MAMs), shortens the distance between the ER and mitochondria, and reduces IP3R protein abundance through mechanisms involving proteasome- and lysosome-associated degradation pathways. These changes are accompanied by disrupted mitochondrial Ca²⁺ homeostasis, ER stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis. Alleviating ER stress with 4-phenylbutyrate or restoring IP3R expression improves mitochondrial function, reduces apoptosis, and inhibits viral replication. The results also suggested a possible association between NS4B and IP3R, although the underlying mechanism requires further investigation. These findings identify MAM remodeling and IP3R dysregulation as important features of cytopathic BVDV infection and suggest that ER-mitochondrial communication may represent a potential target for antiviral intervention.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Evaluating mastoparan as an adjunct to antibiotics for eradicating bacterial persisters in clinical isolates.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Persisters are a subpopulation of bacteria that survive therapeutic doses of antibiotics. When these antibiotics are removed clinically, these persisters can resuscitate, leading to recurrent infections. Mastoparan is a 14-mer peptide that possess intrinsic antibacterial activity as well as the capacity to trigger bacterial clearance at sites of infection through recruitment of immune cells when applied topically. Given its multifaceted antimicrobial properties, we examined whether supplementing antibiotics with mastoparan enhances clearance of persisters among clinical bacterial isolates. In vitro studies indicated that surviving bacterial populations in various clinical isolates of Escherichia coli were able to resume growth when exposed to either mastoparan (minimal bactericidal concentrations of 32-64 μg/mL) or meropenem (20 μg/mL), a potent broad-spectrum antibiotic, individually. However, no resuscitation was detected with any strain when both agents were combined, suggesting that the mastoparan-meropenem combination prevents regrowth of surviving populations. We then examined the effectiveness of meropenem-mastoparan combination against these persisters, in the presence of host cells. As mastoparan was cytotoxic to macrophages at minimal bactericidal concentrations (32-64 µg/mL) in vitro, a sub-therapeutic dose (8 µg/mL) was used to examine the effects of meropenem-mastoparan combination on the various E. coli isolates infecting differentiated THP-1 macrophages. Mastoparan shows limited effects on intracellular bacteria at sub-therapeutic doses and no indications of potentiation when combined with meropenem. Collectively, mastoparan has direct bactericidal effects and shows promise in preventing persister regrowth when combined with antibiotics, but it is largely ineffective at eradicating bacteria within macrophages at sub-therapeutic doses.IMPORTANCEBacterial persisters cause antibiotic failure and infection relapse because they survive treatment and can regrow once drugs are removed. Finding ways to eliminate these cells is critical for improving patient outcomes. Mastoparan, a peptide from wasp venom, has both direct antibacterial activity and the ability to stimulate immune responses, making it an attractive candidate as an antibiotic enhancer. In this study, we show that mastoparan can prevent persister resuscitation when combined with antibiotics in laboratory cultures, but it loses this advantage inside immune cells at doses that are safe for the host. This highlights an important gap between laboratory potency and real-world effectiveness and provides a practical framework for assessing future persister-targeting therapies under clinically relevant conditions.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Gut microbiome stability and mycotoxin degradation confer aflatoxin B1 tolerance in Folsomia candida (Collembola).
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a potent carcinogen that contaminates food and feed, causing significant economic losses and health problems in animals. Soil-dwelling arthropods such as Collembola often coexist with molds and are thought to tolerate toxic fungi, yet their responses to mycotoxins remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of AFB1 on Folsomia candida. We found that AFB1 exposure caused dose-dependent increases in mortality, reductions in body size, and declines in reproductive output of this species. Remarkably, the growth retardation induced by AFB1 was largely alleviated upon removal of AFB1 from the diet. Analysis of gut microbial communities showed that high concentrations of AFB1 had little effect on overall community composition; the gut microbiota was dominated by the phyla Pseudomonadota and Bacillota and by the genera Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Enterobacter. Metagenomic profiling suggested that Wolbachia possesses the potential capability against AFB1. Furthermore, a large proportion of culturable gut bacterial isolates were found to be tolerant of AFB1 and could degrade it to varying degrees. Thus, while high AFB1 levels negatively affect F. candida's fitness, they do not perturb its gut bacterial community and its ability to degrade AFB1, indicating an adaptation of this host-microbiome system to AFB1 exposure. [IMPORTANCE] Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a widespread mycotoxin that threatens food safety and animal health, but how soil animals tolerate AFB1 remains poorly understood. We show that the soil springtail F. candida is highly tolerant to AFB1 even though high doses reduce survival, growth, and reproduction. Notably, AFB1 exposure caused little change in gut microbial community structure. In addition, many gut bacterial isolates tolerated AFB1 and degraded it in vitro. These results suggest that microbiome stability and microbial detoxification capacity may help F. candida persist in mycotoxin-contaminated environments. Our study also highlights toxin-tolerant soil animals as a potential source of microorganisms and functions for aflatoxin biodegradation.

Microbiological Research.title: Adaptive denitrification performance and underlying mechanisms of Pseudomonas stutzeri BBW831 under cadmium stress: EPS remodeling, pH-driven surface adsorption, and transcriptomic reprogramming.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Cadmium (Cd²⁺) strongly interferes with microbial nitrogen removal. This study investigated the denitrification performance, physiological responses, and molecular adaptations of Pseudomonas stutzeri BBW831 under Cd²⁺ stress up to 30 mg/L. Although Cd²⁺ exposure inhibited bacterial growth and markedly delayed nitrate removal, approximately 150 mg/L NO₃⁻-N was ultimately removed at all tested Cd²⁺ concentrations. However, persistent NO₂⁻-N accumulation at 30 mg/L Cd²⁺ (39.99 mg/L at the end of cultivation) indicated impaired downstream denitrification. Consistently, the activities of nitrate reductase and nitrite reductase decreased, with a more pronounced inhibition of nitrite reductase, accompanied by reductions in catalase, superoxide dismutase, and total antioxidant capacity. Cd²⁺ exposure also induced concentration-dependent changes in extracellular polymeric substances (EPS): EPS production peaked at 10 mg/L Cd²⁺ (123.55 ± 6.88 mg/g VSS), whereas higher concentrations reduced EPS production but increased the protein-to-polysaccharide ratio from 56:44-92:8. Three-dimensional excitation-emission matrix spectroscopy further revealed enhanced tryptophan-like protein fluorescence under Cd²⁺ stress. Surface characterization indicated Cd-associated signals and alterations in cell-envelope functional groups, while culture alkalinization suggested a potential contribution of pH-dependent surface interactions to Cd²⁺ binding. Transcriptomic analysis identified 681 differentially expressed genes, revealing extensive metabolic reprogramming. Genes associated with metal efflux, sulfur metabolism, Fe-S cluster assembly, and cell-envelope remodeling were upregulated, whereas multiple genes involved in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and nitrogen metabolism were downregulated. Such expression patterns were further validated by RT-qPCR. These findings provide insights into the adaptive responses of aerobic denitrifiers in Cd²⁺-containing environments and demonstrate the potential of strain BBW831 for Cd²⁺-polluted wastewater remediation.

Microbiological Research.title: Sterol-mediated control of conidiation via FgErg3B in Fusarium graminearum.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Conidia (asexual spores) are the primary inoculum driving the spread of Fusarium head blight, yet chemical inhibition of conidiation in Fusarium graminearum and its underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the ergosterol biosynthetic enzyme FgErg3B as a direct molecular target of pregnenolone, a steroid that strongly inhibits conidiation in F. graminearum. Deletion of FgERG3B reduced conidiation and abolished the response to pregnenolone, while microscale thermophoresis confirmed a high-affinity interaction between pregnenolone and FgErg3B in vitro. Structural modeling, molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis further identified a hydrophobic pocket involved in pregnenolone binding. Further, lipidomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed coordinated changes in lipid metabolism following pregnenolone treatment or FgERG3B deletion, including reduced abundance of four triacylglycerol species and downregulated expression of eight lipid-droplet-associated genes. These findings link FgErg3B to lipid-droplet homeostasis and provide a possible metabolic connection between sterol metabolism and asexual development. Our study identifies FgErg3B as a molecular target for selective inhibition of conidiation and provides a basis for developing strategies to limit Fusarium disease dissemination through targeted suppression of conidial development.

Microbiological Research.title: Co-inoculation with Bacillus velezensis and Acinetobacter baumannii enhances crop Fe uptake in calcareous soils.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), known for their complementary functions and robust stability, are emerging as promising alternatives to single-strain microbial agents. Although the cross-feeding strategy has been widely applied to guide the design of SynComs for sustainable agriculture, its potential to enhance iron (Fe) biofortification for plants remains unexplored. This study aimed to construct a two-strain consortium centered on the beneficial rhizobacterium Bacillus velezensis SQR9 using a cross-feeding strategy, investigate the positive interactions between the two strains in promoting plant Fe uptake, and elucidate the mechanisms underlying their cross-feeding. The results showed that SQR9 engages in bidirectional cross-feeding with Acinetobacter baumannii H3. Compared with individual cultures, their co-culture significantly stimulated the growth of both strains. Furthermore, H3 significantly promoted the biofilm formation of SQR9 and potentiated its root colonization capacity. Crucially, pot experiments confirmed that co-inoculation with SQR9 and H3 more effectively promoted Fe uptake and growth of crops cultivated in calcareous soils. Metabolomic analyses further revealed that SQR9 and H3 mutually support each other's growth through the exchange of specific metabolites, such as α-aspartylphenylalanine and DL-tryptophan. In conclusion, our findings broaden the application prospects of SQR9 as a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium (PGPR) in sustainable agriculture and provide critical theoretical guidance for the rational design of SynComs aimed at enhancing Fe nutrition in crops.

Microbiological Research.title: Stage-specific DNA 6 mA dynamics and metabolic remodeling during lipid accumulation in Mucor circinelloides WJ11.
Microbiological Research.abstract: N⁶-methyladenine (6 mA) dynamics during microbial lipid accumulation remain poorly understood. In this study, 6mA-IP-seq profiles and transcriptomic changes were characterized across four fermentation stages of Mucor circinelloides WJ11, generating a time-resolved catalogue of candidate 6mA-enriched regions in an oleaginous fungus. Global 6 mA levels progressively declined from 0.40% to 0.25%, as quantified by HPLC-MS/MS and supported by dot blot analysis. Genes associated with 6mA-IP-seq peaks were enriched in fatty acid biosynthesis pathways. At the metabolic level, nitrogen limitation was accompanied by changes in respiratory-chain-associated protein concentrations, transient NADH accumulation during active lipogenesis, and transcriptional repression of tricarboxylic acid cycle genes. An early decrease in the S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)/S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) molar ratio and reduced expression of putative methyltransferases were also observed, and eight candidate methyltransferases were identified. Based on these temporally coordinated changes, a correlation-based mechanistic framework linking mitochondrial bioenergetics, methyl-donor metabolism, and epigenetic regulation is proposed, providing a foundation for future functional studies and the biotechnological improvement of microbial lipid production.

Journal of Virology.title: Cellular glycan architecture shapes lineage-specific adaptation and antigenic fidelity of seasonal influenza viruses during propagation.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Isolation and propagation of influenza viruses are essential for surveillance, vaccine strain selection, and vaccine production, yet propagation can select adaptive changes that alter viral phenotypes. Whether such adaptation arises unpredictably during isolation or follows constrained trajectories determined by viral genetic background and the cellular environment remains poorly understood. Using clinical A(H3N2) viruses representing co-circulating lineages, we show that propagation-associated adaptation is lineage- and environment-dependent rather than stochastic. Viruses compatible with a given cellular environment propagated with minimal genetic change, whereas restrictive environments reproducibly selected recurrent adaptive pathways. Adaptation converged on loss of the hemagglutinin glycosylation site at residue 165, broadening recognition of structurally distinct α2,6-sialylated N-glycan scaffolds, and producing measurable antigenic displacement detectable by ferret antisera and human post-vaccination plasma. Together, these findings demonstrate that adaptation of seasonal human influenza viruses during propagation is lineage-dependent and nonrandom, with cellular glycan architecture imposing selective constraints that shape adaptive trajectories. Accounting for lineage-specific propagation compatibility could help prioritize viruses that propagate with minimal adaptive change, improving the genetic and antigenic fidelity of viruses used for surveillance and vaccine strain selection. [IMPORTANCE] Influenza surveillance and vaccine strain selection depend on viruses amplified in laboratory cells, yet some viruses remain genetically stable during propagation, whereas others rapidly adapt. We show that these outcomes are not random consequences of virus isolation. Co-circulating influenza virus lineages differ systematically in their compatibility with the same cellular environments, and restrictive environments repeatedly select specific adaptive routes. A recurrent change that eliminates a glycosylation site on the viral hemagglutinin protein broadens recognition of different cellular glycan structures and alters antigenic properties. Thus, viral genetic background and cellular glycan architecture together constrain how influenza viruses adapt during propagation. Recognizing these differences could help preserve the genetic and antigenic fidelity of viruses used for surveillance and vaccine strain selection.

Journal of Virology.title: Broad-spectrum, small-molecule inhibition of coronavirus NSP10/14 exonuclease activity.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Over the past 30 years, highly pathogenic coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV, MERS, and SARS-CoV-2, have emerged and caused disease in the human population. Currently, antivirals are generally developed to be highly specific for a viral protein, making them susceptible to the development of resistant variants and limiting their breadth across viruses. Here, we report a strategy to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting the relatively conserved coronavirus NSP14 exonuclease protein, prioritized for their breadth across divergent viral proteins. Using a FRET-based high-throughput screen of ~50,000 small-molecule compounds, followed by a series of orthogonal assays, we report the identification of a small-molecule inhibitor, ST095455, that targets the NSP10/14 complex. In addition to SARS-CoV-2, ST095455 inhibited the NSP10/14 complexs of five other CoVs, including endemic and seasonal strains. ST095455 displayed low-micromolar IC50 values in biochemical assays and inhibited SARS-CoV-2 replication in Vero E6 and A549-hACE2 cells, as well as primary epithelial ALI cultures, without obvious cytotoxicity. Dose-dependent reductions in viral RNA and infectious titers were observed, and viral RNA sequencing revealed a corresponding increase in viral genome mutations in progeny virus, consistent with impaired NSP14-proofreading activity. These findings demonstrate NSP10/14 complex as a conserved antiviral target and support future development of ST095455 as a pan-CoV antiviral therapeutic.IMPORTANCETo protect against future zoonotic coronavirus outbreaks, the development of broadly acting antivirals is a top priority. Most existing coronavirus therapeutics target SARS-CoV-2 enzymes and frequently display limited activity against genetically divergent coronaviruses. Here, we used a discovery pipeline that prioritized antiviral breadth from the earliest stages of screening and identified a small-molecule inhibitor of the highly conserved NSP10/14 proofreading complex with activity across multiple genetically distinct coronaviruses. Our lead compound suppressed viral replication and disrupted viral genome fidelity, supporting the concept of proofreading inhibition as a viable target of this virus family. These findings provide both a promising antiviral compound and a general strategy for developing countermeasures against future coronavirus-associated diseases.

Journal of Virology.title: TMEM106B mediates ACE2-independent replication of the SARS-CoV-2 S(E484D) variant in airway-derived cell models.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause significant respiratory disease, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although ACE2 is the primary receptor for viral entry, previous studies have identified a naturally occurring, ACE2-independent entry pathway that depends on cell-surface heparan sulfates and the E484D substitution within the receptor-binding domain of Spike (S). In this study, we expand the panel of airway-derived cell lines that support ACE2-independent, S-E484D-dependent entry, and identify the host lysosomal transmembrane protein TMEM106B as the alternative receptor for infection. Specifically, we show that knockout of TMEM106B completely abolishes infection by SARS-CoV-2 SE484D in NCI-H522 and NCI-H661 cells. Ectopic expression of the luminal C-terminal domain (CTD) of TMEM106B, either alone or redirected to the plasma membrane, is sufficient to enable viral entry largely independent of cell-surface heparan sulfates in non-permissive cells. We show that S-E484D is required for TMEM106B utilization, whereas other variant of concern substitutions at S-E484 are unable to mediate entry. Fc-TMEM106B-CTD fusion protein binds to a chimeric VSV-SARS-CoV-2 SE484D with a higher affinity than WT virus and blocks infection by SARS-CoV-2 SE484D, supporting a direct interaction between S-E484D and TMEM106B-CTD. Serial passaging experiments with VSV-SARS-CoV-2 SE484D identify a V951A mutation within the heptad repeat 1 region that enhances viral spread and fusogenicity in the ACE2-independent cell models. Together, these findings demonstrate that TMEM106B is a key mediator of a naturally occurring ACE2-independent pathway in multiple airway-derived cell lines, and suggest that variation in the S protein can expand receptor usage by SARS-CoV-2. [IMPORTANCE] Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to acquire mutations in the viral spike (S) protein as it circulates in humans. How these mutations influence the cell and tissue tropism of SARS-CoV-2 remains poorly understood. While ACE2 is the canonical host cell receptor for SARS-CoV-2, previous studies revealed the presence of a naturally occurring ACE2-independent entry pathway in multiple airway-derived cell lines that can be utilized only by a SARS-CoV-2 variant bearing the E484D substitution within the viral S protein. Here, we expand the airway-derived cell line models that support ACE2-independent and S-E484D-dependent entry and show that the host lysosomal transmembrane protein, TMEM106B, is an essential viral entry factor. Although the E484D substitution is currently rare in human isolates, our findings raise the possibility that even single mutations in SARS-CoV-2 S can allow the utilization of alternative entry pathways that broaden its cell and tissue tropism.

Journal of Virology.title: PEDV S protein induces CMPK2 to activate cGAS-STING and NLRP3 antiviral signaling through MLS-dependent mitochondrial localization.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a threat to the global swine industry, yet how PEDV-encoded proteins regulate mitochondria-associated innate antiviral immunity remains unclear. Here, we identify the PEDV spike (S) protein as an upstream inducer of cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase 2 (CMPK2) expression. Viral protein screening and domain-mapping analyses showed that the S protein induced CMPK2 expression through type I interferon (IFN-I)-related signaling and interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), while its N-terminal S1⁰ region retained the ability to induce CMPK2 expression. The antiviral function of CMPK2 required mitochondrial localization mediated by its mitochondrial localization signal (MLS). As a rate-limiting enzyme in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) synthesis, CMPK2 contributed to mtDNA homeostasis. PEDV infection induced mitochondrial dysfunction and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) accumulation. Under these conditions, CMPK2 was critical for the generation and cytosolic release of oxidized mtDNA (ox-mtDNA). Cytosolic ox-mtDNA acted as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) to activate the cGAS-STING pathway and the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby restricting PEDV replication. Deletion of the MLS disrupted the mitochondrial localization of CMPK2, impaired its regulation of mtDNA homeostasis, and largely abolished its immunostimulatory and antiviral activities. Moreover, S protein-induced activation of cGAS-STING and the NLRP3 inflammasome was markedly attenuated in CMPK2-KO cells. Collectively, our findings reveal that the PEDV S protein engages CMPK2-dependent mitochondrial antiviral immunity and establish that MLS-mediated mitochondrial localization of CMPK2 is essential for ox-mtDNA generation, cytosolic release, and innate immune activation. [IMPORTANCE] Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) causes severe diarrhea in pigs and substantial economic losses, but which viral proteins trigger protective host responses remains unclear. We show that the viral spike protein activates host defense signaling and increases the expression of cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase 2, a mitochondrial host defense factor. This factor promotes the generation and cytosolic release of oxidized mitochondrial DNA, which activates antiviral and inflammatory defenses that limit viral replication. Its localization within mitochondria is essential for these protective effects. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized immunoregulatory role for the spike protein and show how a viral structural protein can engage mitochondrial DNA metabolism to strengthen host defense. These findings establish an MLS-dependent role for CMPK2 in mtDNA-associated antiviral immunity during PEDV infection.

PLOS Biology.title: Distinct trajectories and predictability of individual grouping patterns in dolphins link social ageing to longevity
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Kelley C. Meehan, Barbara Class, Shinichi Nakagawa, Meredith MacQueeney, Vivienne Foroughirad, Janet Mann, Celine H. Frère Recent work has unearthed strong relationships between ageing and average sociability. Clear patterns of decreases in average sociability are observed across taxa; many of these are sex-specific. Individuals, however, generally deviate from population averages, and discounting individual variance in behaviour could disguise mechanisms of adaptation, selection, and developmental stability. Using 40 years of behavioural data from Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins, we provide new insights into social ageing. We achieve this by simultaneously measuring both mean (repeatability) and variance (predictability) in group size—a trait reflecting social interaction preference—across the population and throughout individual lifespans. Double hierarchical location-scale modelling reveals a multidimensional response; at both the population and individual level, the mean trait response (plasticity) and variance (malleability) of group size change with age. At a population level and for most individuals, average group size increases then declines in later life. This decline is more pronounced in males, though males are consistently in larger and more predictable groups than females at all life stages. Population predictability of group size increases throughout life, consistent with our prediction that social preferences strengthen with age. Individuals which are highly sociable are also highly predictable, and increased sociability and predictability both appear correlated with longevity. The positive correlation between increasing predictability and longevity leads us to hypothesise that individuals develop social competence by refining their social experiences. This process likely involves increasing social selectivity and optimising social choices to achieve a net fitness benefit. These findings provide novel insights into social ageing and illustrate how studying variance in social traits can capture processes of social competence, selectivity, and adaptation of social phenotypes occurring within an individual’s social environment.

PLOS Biology.title: Species diversity increases information flow about predation in bird communities
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Agnishikhe Kumar, Jiahao Wu, Ping Ding, Jakob Bro-Jørgensen, Mylène Dutour, Ari E. Martínez, Xingfeng Si, Qiang Zhang, Eben Goodale The Biodiversity-Ecosystem Functioning (BEF) literature has shown species diversity to be essential for ecosystem functioning and services. Yet this concept has not been extended often to behavioral ecology, so that although it is understood that acquiring social information from heterospecific individuals is an important component of ecosystem functioning, it is unclear how animal signaling at the community level, and subsequent information flow, is related to increased species diversity. Eliciting vocal responses using predator models across 10 nature reserves on a latitudinal gradient, we first show that the species diversity of birds is correlated with signaling about predation, both in the low-risk system of mobbing and in the higher-risk system of alarm calls. After finding a similar result across a fragment area gradient in one reserve, we used this system to test how interspecific information flow is affected by species diversity. Potential mechanisms behind this effect include that species are complementary in the characteristics of their mobbing calls, so more species translates into more cumulative information, or there are higher signaling rates as more individuals are involved, or a specific keystone species is more likely to occur. This experiment varied the number of species producing mobbing calls (one, two, four, eight species), with two playback construction methods (standardizing call rate, as typical for BEF experiments, or letting it increase with species richness, as in natural assemblages). Heterospecific mobbing participation (number of vocal species, number of participating individuals), and responses (call rate, probability to call in the first minute and frequency range) increased with species richness. Construction method significantly interacted with species richness, as non-standardized exemplars showed accentuated response as species richness increased. These results match expectations that complementary differences among species in the acoustic characteristics of mobbing calls, and increased call rate, both contribute to the result. There was little evidence that the signals of one particular species changed the experimental result. The overall evidence thus supports the hypothesis that the species diversity of a community is a key component influencing the quantity and the characteristics of signaling and information flow inside it.

mBio.title: Obesity-associated changes in immune cell dynamics during alphavirus infection revealed by single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
mBio.abstract: Obesity alters host immunity, resulting in worse disease outcomes following infection with various pathogens, including arthritogenic alphaviruses. However, the impact of obesity on the functional landscape of immune cells during acute arthritogenic alphavirus infection remains incompletely explored. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to dissect the blood and tissue immune responses to Mayaro virus (MAYV) infection in lean and obese mice. Footpad injection of MAYV caused significant shifts in immune cell populations and induced robust expression of interferon response and proinflammatory cytokine genes and related pathways in both blood and tissue. In MAYV-infected lean mice, single-cell analysis of the footpad response revealed a unique macrophage subset (F4/80loMHCII+) with high expression of interferon-responsive genes that was replaced by an alternative, F4/80int population in infected obese mice. Macrophages isolated from lean mice had higher levels of inflammatory gene expression. Furthermore, obese macrophages infected with MAYV and CHIKV ex vivo produce an immunoregulatory response (IL-10) compared to lean macrophages that produce a higher pro-inflammatory response (TNF). The stronger inflammatory response in lean macrophages was associated with less severe systemic disease in lean mice. These results provide evidence for the role of a unique population of macrophages that may contribute to the superior capacity of lean mice to control arthritogenic alphavirus infection.IMPORTANCEArthritogenic alphaviruses-including chikungunya, Mayaro, and Ross River viruses-cause chronic, often disabling joint and muscle disease and are expanding into new regions, yet no approved therapies target the disease process itself. Obesity is a known risk factor for more severe outcomes after infection, but the underlying immune mechanisms have been unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that infection drives widespread interferon and inflammatory responses in blood and infected tissue and that obesity specifically alters the macrophage populations present at the infection site. Lean mice mount a highly activated, interferon-driven macrophage response linked to better control of local inflammation, while obese mice instead accumulate a related but less activated population enriched for necroptosis-associated genes and linked to greater tissue damage. These findings identify a specific macrophage subset as a likely contributor to the more severe alphavirus disease seen with obesity and a potential target for future therapies.
