Identification of a highly conserved neutralization epitope targeting poxvirus F13/F13L homologs across seven genera of the subfamily Chordopoxvirinae, family Poxviridae.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The emergence of the human monkeypox epidemic sparked interest in the development of broadly protective pan-poxvirus vaccines that protect against all members of the Poxviridae family. Here, we describe a B-cell monoclonal antibody (mAb) raised against the lumpy skin disease virus ORF29 protein that demonstrates broad-spectrum cross-binding activity against seven genera in the Chordopoxvirinae subfamily, Poxviridae family. Subsequently, a novel continuous linear and conformational epitope has been systematically identified among poxviruses. Furthermore, alanine-scanning mutagenesis analysis confirmed that five critical amino acids (199IGGVF203) of this novel epitope were highly conserved among poxviruses. Crucially, neutralizing assays revealed that this mAb (ORF293C4-2E9) retained broad-spectrum binding and cross-neutralizing activity against capripoxvirus and orthopoxvirus infections in vitro. In vitro antibody internalization and functional assays demonstrated that full-length IgG from ORF293C4-2E9 exhibited higher neutralizing potency than that of its corresponding Fab fragment at the initial stage of viral attachment. Finally, mouse challenge experiments demonstrated that passive ORF293C4-2E9 transfer and peptide immunization provided cross-protective efficacy against ectromelia virus infection following intranasal injection in vivo. Our research provides experimental evidence for heterosubtypic immunity and demonstrates the feasibility of epitope-based approaches for developing pan-poxvirus vaccines and antiviral drugs. [IMPORTANCE] Similar to the COVID-19 pandemic, the recent global outbreak of human monkeypox highlights the critical need for vaccines and therapeutics that offer broad protection against a range of poxviruses. In this study, we comprehensively describe a monoclonal antibody derived from the lumpy skin disease virus that maintains broad cross-reactive binding and neutralizing activity against various poxviruses, including orthopoxviruses (e.g., monkeypox, vaccinia, and ectromelia) and capripoxviruses. Our study identified a highly conserved epitope within the ORF29 protein and its analogs in seven genera in the subfamily Chordopoxvirinae of the Poxviridae family. Our findings provide the first experimental evidence that heterosubtypic immunity can be achieved through epitope-targeted strategies, thereby paving the way for the development of a universally conserved epitope for a broad-spectrum poxvirus vaccine and antiviral drugs.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Beyond the rat: over a quarter century of disease model integration at the Rat Genome Database.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Rat Genome Database (RGD, https://rgd.mcw.edu) is a multispecies knowledgebase and the primary online resource for genomic, genetic, phenotypic, and disease data for rat. In the past 6 years, RGD has incorporated new data, including three new species, two rat reference genome assemblies, eight rat strain de novo assemblies from Dr Peter Doris' group, and variant data for 118 unique strains from the Hybrid Rat Discovery Panel. Systematic manual curation of metadata and consistent reprocessing of RNA-Seq data from the GEO database have resulted in the addition of a substantial dataset of standardized transcriptomic data. RGD's disease-centric focus has continued with the creation of four new disease portals, bringing the total number of portals up to sixteen and three existing portals have been updated. Four of RGD's data mining and analysis tools were redesigned with a cleaner, more intuitive look and feel and additional functionality. RGD's primary genome browser has been upgraded to JBrowse 2, a browser designed to facilitate analyses across species and between assemblies within a species. To support researchers wanting to learn more about using RGD's tools and data, RGD has begun a project to improve and expand the website's help pages and video tutorials.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Database resources of the National Center for Biotechnology Information in 2027.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) provides biomedical data resources including PubMed®, a repository of citations and abstracts published in life science journals, and ClinicalTrials.gov, a repository of clinical research summaries. NCBI also hosts a multitude of resources providing nucleotide sequences and sequence-derived products, such as proteins and protein structures. Search and retrieval operations are available for most of the 40 distinct repositories, knowledgebases, and services. The E-utilities and NCBI Datasets serve as the programming interface for most of these. Resources receiving significant updates in the past year include PubMed®, PubMed Central® (PMC), SciENcv, ClinicalTrials.gov, ClinVar, dbSNP, dbGaP, GTR, MedGen®, Pathogen Detection and the National Database of Antibiotic Resistant Organisms, and PubChem®. These resources can be accessed through the NCBI home page at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: OMA orthology in 2027: orthology, ancestral gene repertoires, and comparative genomics at scale.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: OMA is a longstanding resource for inferring and exploring orthologous relationships across the tree of life. Here, we describe recent developments that broaden the comparative genomics information and analyses supported by the OMA ecosystem. The latest OMA release contains 2983 extant genomes and 1226 ancestral genome reconstructions spanning all domains of life, with expanded eukaryotic representation and quality-assessed genome selection. We integrated protein structure-aware information across all proteins in OMA, providing structure-derived 3Di representations and structural alignments for hierarchical orthologous groups. For custom datasets, FastOMA enables scalable orthology across thousands of genomes, while OrthoXML-tools facilitates interoperable manipulation and downstream analysis of orthology data. Building on previous resources for ancestral gene repertoire and gene order reconstruction, an extended chromosome viewer enables richer exploration of gene order in extant and reconstructed ancestral genomes, including gene adjacency evolution and integrated downstream analyses. Functional analysis has been extended through the OMA REST API, enabling customizable Gene Ontology enrichment analyses of extant and ancestral gene sets. Finally, updated training resources and support for private deployments broaden access to the OMA ecosystem. Together, these developments provide an integrated framework for studying gene families and genome evolution from sequences, structures, and evolutionary context. OMA is freely accessible at https://omabrowser.org/.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Beyond profiles: Supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Kaiyu Qiu, Jan Ludwiczak, Andrei N. Lupas, Stanislaw Dunin-Horkawicz Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey β-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Vascular modelling of peripheral ischaemic disease response
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Lachlan Arthur, Michele Carrabba, Paolo Madeddu, Steven McDougall, Vassilis Sboros Ischaemic disease presents a significant challenge in medical science due to its widespread manifestations in the body and its tendency to only become overt in its late stages, beyond where current intervention methods are effective. Diseases such as coronary heart disease and peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent leading causes of death and are detrimental to quality of life. Focussing on the latter, PAD incurs an amputation rate of around 25%, largely owing to microvascular disease that prevents tissue recovery even after revascularisation. Current methods for investigating PAD either cannot chart specific vascular determinants, such as with in vivo imaging, or deform and remove subjects from longitudinal studies, such as with ex vivo tissue sampling. Presented to aid live research, computational modelling can collate information and build models of ischaemia using available information and provide a reasonable approximation of the disease’s chronology and thus support understanding and advance research of PAD. Proposed here, is a 3D in silico model of ischaemic disease in the limb using a system of purpose-built platforms. Starting with a real micro-computed tomography image of the murine hindlimb, a realistic vessel bed was generated using vascular graphing software, ViGiL. From here, the model was realised in a defined pressure gradient via flow-modelling software, numPTI. With the base model of lower limb arteries, collateral vasculature was generated throughout the vessel space. This provides a bypass system for adaptation post-ischaemia. Upon ischaemic induction, the collateral bed responds to the loss of flow and successfully adapted to recover flow with similar density and distribution of diameters in collateral arterioles (p>> 0.05). Moreover, a satisfactory flow recovery of 50% was achieved after 6 days, showing that the model can reflect the specific vascular environment in which disease is incited. The proceeds of this study lay the groundwork for truly realistic ischaemic models including moving towards a predictive model than can signify when and where key indicators of PAD manifest.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: CoEVFold suite: User friendly pipelines to visually represent protein coevolution
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Chris L. B. Graham, Liam Cremona, Robin Little, Christopher D. A. Rodrigues Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) data underlies current principles in protein folding and protein-protein interaction prediction, from which deep-learning models trained on protein sequence and structure datasets can predict protein structure. However, what is missing are user-friendly tools that enable researchers to identify and visualise coevolution, the principal signal that these MSAs encode. Here we present tools to identify and visualize coevolution, through a pipeline (CoEVFold) that uses basic direct coupling algorithms derived from GREMLIN and an input alignment of sequences from MMseqs2. We also provide notebooks to calculate coevolution with alternative methods such as CCMpred or plmc. The pipeline generates a visual representation of coevolution for a single protein but can also represent coevolution of homomeric or heteromeric protein complexes, as well as coevolution within protein networks. The input for this pipeline can be an amino acid sequence, or protein structures from AlphaFold/RoseTTAFold, the user’s own files or the PDB. Using proteins from well-studied prokaryotic and eukaryotic model systems (Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae), as well as phage proteins, we show that CoEVFold detects coevolution between proteins known to interact, between protomers of known oligomers, and within known protein complexes. Benchmarked against 18 heteromeric complexes of known structure, the top-ranked inter-protein couplings identified interface contacts with a precision of 0.8 or more in 7 complexes, and CoEVMapper rankings agreed with STRING associations for an Escherichia coli cell-wall synthesis network (ROC AUC 0.72–0.74). For homo-oligomers, the top-ranked coevolution pairs not explained by the monomer structure were protomer–protomer contacts in 25% (SpoIIIE) and 47% (MlaD) of cases, against 2% or less expected by chance. The coupling calculation for a ~ 950-residue complex took 114 s with GREMLIN, compared with 116 s for CCMpred and 2,060 s for plmc. Collectively, this suite of tools, named ‘CoEVFold suite’, has broad applicability and provide a useful toolkit to those interested in dissecting protein-protein interactions and networks.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Deciphering the replication-division coordination in E. coli: A unified mathematical framework for systematic model comparison
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Alexandre Perrin, Marie Doumic, Meriem El Karoui, Sylvie Méléard Despite extensive research, the quantitative principles that govern the coordination between DNA replication and cell division in bacteria remain debated. Multiple theoretical models have been proposed, some postulating that a single regulatory process is sufficient to ensure replication–division coordination, while others argue that two concurrent processes are required for robust control. In this work, we develop a unifying mathematical framework within which models can be consistently formulated, qualitatively analysed and quantitatively compared. This framework also allows us to propose a new double-process model. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions under which single-process models can reproduce physiological cell behaviours. Beyond the correlation-based analyses extensively used to date, we further demonstrate within a comprehensive statistical framework that double-process models more accurately recapitulate experimental data across all growth conditions. Specifically, the new model we propose robustly captures the replication-division coordination in every growth regime, thereby providing a foundation for future mechanistic studies.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Differential vulnerability of stimulus-locked and persistent gamma oscillations: Implications in schizophrenia
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Daniel W. Chung, G. Bard Ermentrout Working memory depends on gamma oscillations generated across sensory and prefrontal cortices. In primary visual cortex (V1), stimulus-locked gamma oscillations encode stimulus information, while in prefrontal cortex (PFC), persistent gamma oscillations maintain this information after the stimulus is removed. In schizophrenia (SZ), gamma power is reduced in both V1 and PFC, consistent with deficits in sensory encoding and working memory maintenance. Both oscillation regimes arise from a canonical microcircuit involving pyramidal neurons (PNs) and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs). Yet, whether the two regimes are similarly or differentially vulnerable to synaptic alterations within this circuit in SZ remains unknown. To investigate this question, we used a mean-field model of the PN-PVI circuit, in which the two regimes were distinguished by NMDA conductance values reflecting the difference in GluN2B expression between human PFC and V1. We then assessed three synaptic alterations quantified using molecular and structural proxies in postmortem SZ brains: lower excitatory inputs to PVIs (E→I), lower inhibitory inputs to PNs (I→E), and greater variability in E→I strength. Each alteration produced larger gamma power deficits in the persistent regime than in the stimulus-locked regime. Applied together, these alterations interacted synergistically to reduce gamma power, with the persistent regime exhibiting a more pronounced deficit. Bifurcation analyses revealed that this differential vulnerability arises from a wider margin of oscillatory stability in the stimulus-locked regime, and that reduced I→E strength additionally abolished the bistability required for the persistent regime. These findings predict that a larger magnitude of synaptic alteration is required to disrupt gamma oscillations in V1 than in PFC, consistent with postmortem reports of more severe alterations in V1 in SZ. Together, they establish a differential vulnerability model of cortical gamma oscillations in SZ, in which regional differences in oscillatory stability determine how much synaptic alteration is required to disrupt oscillations with distinct dynamics.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: TRAFIKK: Systematic prediction and mechanistic interpretation of anticancer drug synergies
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Marco Fariñas, Viviam Bermúdez, Eirini Tsirvouli, Kristine Lippestad, John Zobolas, Tero Aittokallio, Kaisa Lehti, Åsmund Flobak Effective drug combination therapies can improve cancer treatment, yet the mechanistic basis of drug synergy remains poorly understood. Most computational approaches prioritise predictive accuracy over molecular mechanistic interpretability, providing limited insights into how synergistic effects emerge across signalling contexts. We developed Trafikk, a molecular-signalling network-based framework that simulates drug perturbations in cell-line-specific computational models to mirror functional outcomes in experimental combination screens. Across two independent large-scale datasets, Trafikk identified synergistic combinations with >77% recall. Functional response predictions revealed both conserved and context-dependent mechanisms. While AKT-MEK co-inhibition consistently disrupted coordinated survival and apoptotic signalling in 742 cell lines, PI3K-BCL2 synergy arose through distinct death programs shaped by cell-context-specific network constraints. Trafikk combines predictive performance with mechanistic interpretability, capturing how and why drug synergy emerges across cellular contexts. Source code, installation instructions and usage tutorial are freely available at https://github.com/druglogics/trafikk.

Biogeosciences.title: Effects of enhanced rock weathering on soil gas fluxes across UK land uses
Biogeosciences.abstract: Effects of enhanced rock weathering on soil gas fluxes across UK land uses Kate Rees, Maria Val Martin, David Beerling, Aurelia Bezanger, Nicholas Cowan, Ruby Devlin, Mark Hanlon, Ben Langford, Sergiy Medinets, and Julia Drewer Biogeosciences, 23, 8577–8598, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8577-2026, 2026 Enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed rock on soil to capture CO₂. We tested how this affects gases released from different UK soils in a lab study. Results varied with land uses: some soils released less CO₂ or more nitric oxide, others showed small changes in methane or other gases. This understanding of a wide range of trace gases is crucial to examine climate forcing and air quality implications of enhanced rock weathering deployment.
