Annual Review of Genetics.title: From Determinants to Condensates: Revisiting the Function of Germ Granules.
Annual Review of Genetics.abstract: Germ granules are RNA-protein assemblies that segregate to the primordial germ cells (PGCs) in embryos. Germ granules are often considered cell fate determinants, yet not all animals use germ granules to specify germ cell fate. The function of germ granules is of renewed interest now that they are recognized as biomolecular condensates, cellular compartments that assemble without limiting membranes. We highlight common features of germ granules in Drosophila melanogaster, Caenorhabditis elegans, and Danio rerio, including a core shell architecture, complex mRNA composition, and concentration of PIWI-class Argonautes. These features suggest that a primary role of germ granules is to transmit condensate-based epigenetic programs across generations. Germ granules were also co-opted as vehicles for RNA localization by a small group of transcripts required to launch the germline, including Nanos. We suggest that this secondary function may have led to specializations in germ granule architecture to accommodate species-specific constraints on mRNA regulation.

Annual Review of Genetics.title: The Role of Transposable Elements in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
Annual Review of Genetics.abstract: The molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases remain incompletely understood, hindering the development of disease-modifying therapies. Therefore, new conceptual frameworks for neurodegeneration are urgently needed. This review examines evidence suggesting that transposable elements (TEs) play a role in these diseases. Aberrant TE activation has been reported in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and multiple sclerosis, and it is increasingly linked to innate immune activation, genomic instability, and neuronal dysfunction. Due to their repetitive nature, TEs are difficult to study. However, recent advances in sequencing technologies now enable more precise profiling of TE expression and activity in the aging and diseased brain. In this review, we discuss recent findings and key methodological and bioinformatic challenges. We also highlight emerging models that position TEs as potential drivers of chronic neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration, with important implications for the development of novel biomarkers and therapeutic strategies for these currently incurable diseases.

Annual Review of Genetics.title: RNA-Guided Genome Organization Across Scales.
Annual Review of Genetics.abstract: The genome is hierarchically folded, from one-dimensional organization along the chromatin fiber involving nucleosomes, epigenetic marks, and proteins to three-dimensional regulatory element-driven chromatin loops and large chromatin domains. These layers are spatially coordinated with nuclear bodies to shape genome organization in a spatiotemporal manner. Genome folding is not a static architectural outcome but rather an actively regulated process requiring the coordinated action of diverse molecular factors across scales. Although DNA sequence, histone modifications, and proteins have traditionally been viewed as the primary determinants of genome organization, RNA has recently emerged as an integral regulatory layer shaping genome architecture. Beyond serving as a transcriptional output, RNA functions as an active organizational component that modulates chromatin structure, stabilizes regulatory interactions, and coordinates molecular assemblies within the nucleus. In this review, we present a conceptual framework for RNA-mediated genome organization across scales, emphasizing unifying principles rather than individual molecular players or RNA classes while drawing on selected well-studied examples for illustration.

Annual Review of Genetics.title: Transcript Direct Repair: RNA-Guided Pathways of DNA Double-Strand Break Repair.
Annual Review of Genetics.abstract: The Central Dogma of molecular biology has traditionally emphasized a unidirectional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein, with RNA-to-DNA information transfer being viewed as a specialized process associated primarily with selfish genetic elements or telomere maintenance. However, emerging evidence demonstrates that endogenous RNA directly participates in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair. We synthesize these findings within the framework of transcript direct repair (TDR), defining pathways in which transcripts serve as genetic templates or structural scaffolds to facilitate repair. We highlight how eukaryotic DNA polymerases, including Pol θ and Pol ζ, utilize intrinsic reverse transcriptase activity for RNA-templated DNA synthesis independent of viral enzymes. By unifying RNA-templated homologous recombination and RNA-mediated end-joining mechanisms, we establish TDR as a crucial, physiological component of genome maintenance. Finally, we discuss TDR's evolutionary implications, such as whole-intron deletions, illustrating how endogenous transcription shapes long-term genome remodeling.

Annual Review of Genetics.title: The Genetics of Sleep Regulation in Mice.
Annual Review of Genetics.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet the mechanisms that generate sleep states and encode the need for sleep are not yet fully understood. Mouse genetics has begun to transform these mechanisms into testable problems by linking specific genes and circuits to vigilance-state dynamics. Here, we review forward-genetic approaches that have uncovered unanticipated regulators as well as reverse-genetic strategies accelerated by CRISPR and adult brain-wide adeno-associated virus (AAV) perturbation. Recent work converges on phosphorylation-centered control of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS), exemplified by the SIK3-HDAC4 pathway and related kinase-phosphatase networks. We discuss how neuromodulators orchestrate vigilance states through circuit- and receptor-dependent mechanisms and discuss emerging roles of ion channels, astrocytes, and microglia. Finally, we address methodological constraints in mouse sleep phenotyping and genetic manipulation that shape the interpretation of sleep phenotypes.

mSystems.title: Intratumoral Peptostreptococcus stomatis promotes the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma through the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK pathway.
mSystems.abstract: The intratumoral microbiome is increasingly implicated in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet its compositional features and functional contributions remain incompletely defined. Here, through an integrated meta-analysis of nine public 16S rRNA sequencing data sets encompassing 578 samples, we revealed a significantly dysbiotic intratumoral microbiota in OSCC, characterized by reduced α-diversity and distinct β-diversity. Machine learning confirmed the diagnostic potential of this microbial signature, achieving an average cross-validation area under the curve of 0.83. Among the tumor-enriched taxa, Peptostreptococcus stomatis was consistently identified, and its intratumoral enrichment was validated by fluorescent in situ hybridization in clinical specimens. Functionally, P. stomatis enhances OSCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and accelerates tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model. Mechanistically, we demonstrated that P. stomatis directly adheres to OSCC cells and activates the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK signaling axis. Genetic ablation of Erbb2 abrogated P. stomatis-induced malignant phenotypes in vitro and tumor growth in vivo, establishing ERBB2 as an essential mediator of this oncogenic pathway. Collectively, our findings establish P. stomatis as a functionally significant driver of OSCC progression, unveiling the bacterium and its host interaction interface as promising targets for microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutic intervention.IMPORTANCEThe role of the intratumoral microbiome in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly defined. Through a large-scale meta-analysis of 578 samples, we reveal a consistent microbial dysbiosis in OSCC and establish Peptostreptococcus stomatis as a functionally significant driver of tumor progression. We demonstrate that P. stomatis directly activates the integrin α6/β4-ERBB2-MAPK signaling axis, and that genetic ablation of ERBB2 abrogates its oncogenic effects. These findings position P. stomatis and its host interaction interface as promising targets for microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutic intervention in OSCC.

mSystems.title: Rhizosphere microbiome transplantation: restoring plant health through community coalescence.
mSystems.abstract: There is growing interest in holistic, community-level approaches for engineering the rhizosphere microbiome to improve plant health and resilience under environmental stress. Rhizosphere microbiome transplantation (RMT) has emerged as an advanced strategy within this framework, characterized by the transfer of an entire donor-derived microbial community into stressed or degraded soils to restore plant-beneficial functions, an approach conceptually analogous to fecal microbiota transplantation used for correcting gut dysbiosis. Unlike reductionist single-strain or synthetic/defined-community inoculants, whole-community transplantation preserves the ecological complexity of naturally assembled microbiomes. Its theoretical foundation lies in community coalescence, whereby introduced and resident microbiota interact to form a newly structured community rather than one simply replacing the other. While RMT has been previously noted briefly or discussed as one of several microbiome engineering strategies, no review to date has comprehensively synthesized its effects across the full range of biotic and abiotic stresses alongside its ecological and molecular basis. Here, we critically synthesize recent evidence based on primary RMT studies published from 2018 through 2026 for its effects across three functional domains-disease suppression, abiotic stress tolerance, and plant growth promotion, and examine the mechanisms underlying transplantation success, including network architecture and host-mediated recruitment. We further outline key bottlenecks constraining widespread adoption, spanning ecological contingency, lack of standardized protocols, and incomplete mechanistic understanding, and propose recommendations for advancing RMT from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward predictable, field-ready practice.

Cell.title: A shared interbacterial membrane underlies mycobacterial cording
authors: Marlen Petersen, Richa Mishra, Miriam S. Weber, Anna Rafalik, Bibek Acharya, Turner P. Brown, Vera Lechner, Clément Bousquet, Melanie Hoos, Alexandra Kummer, Eugenia Guerrero Aruffo, Casey Papson, Alex Aboagye, Bei Shi Lee, Sönke Sdunnus, Michael Berney, Melanie Hannebelle, Margot Riggi, Benjamin M. Swarts, Matthieu Chavent, Wonpil Im, Gregor L. Weiss, Vivek V. Thacker
Cell.abstract: Cording is a century-old mycobacterial virulence trait. CryoET and light microscopy reveal that incomplete cell separation during division generates a shared interbacterial membrane. Membrane sharing provides the mechanistic basis for cording, an explanation for mechanical resilience, and a new picture of the mycomembrane in supracellular architectures distinct from planktonic bacteria.

Cell.title: Cardiomyocyte-derived circulating extracellular vesicles enable a non-invasive liquid biopsy of human myocardium
authors: Priyanka Gokulnath, Michail Spanos, Elizabeth Hutchins, Bessie Meechoovet, Quanhu Sheng, Phillip Lin, Michael J. Betti, Kaushik V. Amancherla, Emeli Chatterjee, Marta Garcia-Contreras, Ritin Sharma, Natacha Carnel-Amar, Balazs Kazala, Claire Lin, Sameeksha Tiwari, Sary F. Aranki, Joshua M. Gorham, Christopher Azzam, Ima Ghaeli, José Fabian Victorino, Krystine Garcia-Mansfield, Ryan Pfeffer, Parul Sahu, Brian R. Lindman, Sammy Elmariah, Xavier Bledsoe, Michelle L. Lance, Tarek Absi, Yan Ru Su, Ngoc Do, Dimitrios Varrias, Michail Kladas, Miroslav Radulovic, Dimitris Tsiachris, Anastasios Spanos, Konstantinos Tsioufis, Jonathan G. Seidman, Christine E. Seidman, Patrick T. Ellinor, Nathan R. Tucker, James L. Januzzi, Patrick Pirrotte, Tijana Jovanovic-Talisman, Jochen D. Muehlschlegel, Guoping Li, Eric R. Gamazon, Kendall Van Keuren-Jensen, Ravi Shah, Saumya Das
Cell.abstract: This study develops an approach to selectively capture cardiomyocyte-derived circulating extracellular vesicles (cardiovesicles) from plasma. Cardiovesicle RNAs dynamically track disease-specific cardiomyocyte transcriptional states and reflect genetic liability for cardiovascular disease, providing a non-invasive window into the molecular state of the human heart, suggesting a path toward personalized cardiovascular medicine.

Current Biology.title: Ventral striatal dopamine increases following hippocampal sharp-wave ripples
authors: Miriam A. Janssen, Hung-tu Chen, Nicolas X. Tritsch, Matthijs A.A. van der Meer
Current Biology.abstract: Janssen et al. show that transient increases in ventral striatal dopamine follow hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) in mice. SWR-linked dopamine transients are smaller than reward prediction errors, scale with SWR properties, and are preferentially expressed during offline rest, providing a candidate mechanism linking internally generated hippocampal activity to downstream evaluation.

Current Biology.title: Flashing light modulates insect behavior in a species-specific manner
authors: Md Saheb Ali, Xinyi Luo, David D. Au, Todd C. Holmes
Current Biology.abstract: Ali et al. show that rapidly flashing ultraviolet light promotes light avoidance and reshapes daily spatiotemporal behavioral organization across Drosophila species. These responses depend on opsin-based photoreceptors, Cryptochrome and the circadian clock, with PDF+ lateral ventral clock neurons integrating light inputs to shape behavioral responses.

Water Research.title: Microbially mediated groundwater ammonium dynamics across redox zonation: Hydrogeochemical and metabolic constraints.
Water Research.abstract: Groundwater ammonium (NH4N) enrichment poses a major water-quality risk and ecological threat in arid and semi-arid regions, yet microbial mechanisms governing its dynamics across redox zonation remain underexplored. This study combined hydrogeochemical and isotopic investigations with metagenomic analyses to determine how microbially mediated source-sink processes regulate NH4N dynamics under contrasting redox conditions. Along the groundwater flow path from the lake-distal suboxic zone (G1) to the nearshore reducing zone (G2), nitrate (NO3N) declined markedly as NH4N accumulated progressively. Hydrogeochemical and isotopic evidence suggested that nitrification and anammox were associated with enhanced NH4N removal in the G1. In the G2, denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) potentially contributed to NO3N attenuation, whereas mineralization of nitrogen-containing OM and DNRA showed enhanced potential to promote in situ NH4N enrichment. Metagenomic and metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) analyses confirmed pronounced redox-driven functional partitioning. Enrichment of nitrification- and anammox-related genes (nxrA/B, hzsA/C and hao/hzo) in G1 indicated the metabolic potential for efficient NH4N removal. In contrast, genes associated with ammonification, nitrogen fixation, DNRA, and denitrification (gdhA, nrfA/H, nifD/H/K and napA/B) were co-enriched in G2, supporting enhanced functional potential for coupled NO3N attenuation and NH4N enrichment. PLS-SEM modeling further demonstrated that redox zonation reorganized microbial nitrogen transformation pathways along the groundwater flow path, shifting the system from oxidative NH4N consumption in G1 to reductive NH4N enrichment in G2. These findings reveal a redox-controlled microbial mechanism contributing to groundwater NH4N dynamics, with important implications for zone-specific management of nitrogen pollution in arid and semi-arid regions.

Water Research.title: Making waves: Toward a stability-first framework for durable AOP-ceramic membrane systems in authentic water matrices.
Water Research.abstract: Catalytic ceramic membranes that couple advanced oxidation with physical separation offer an attractive single-unit solution for water treatment. Although catalytic ceramic membrane systems have demonstrated promising performance in laboratory studies and pilot-scale applications, their engineering deployment remains limited. A major unresolved challenge is the lack of a consistent system-level approach for evaluating and managing long-term stability under realistic water matrices and operational disturbances. In authentic water matrices, fouling, scaling, and catalyst poisoning collectively shorten membrane life in ways that short-term lab tests fail to capture. The discussion focuses on three barriers to application-oriented transformation, including interference from natural organic matter and inorganic ions, real-world operating challenges (pressure fluctuations, vibration, harsh cleaning), and insufficient long-term stability data from short-term idealized studies. Within this stability-first perspective, system-level stability is considered across four interacting dimensions: catalytic stability, hydraulic stability, structural stability, and functional recoverability. The article then outlines current stability-enhancement strategies, including protective coatings, pore-structure engineering, and online cleaning, and notes that each carries inherent limitations. Critically, a major obstacle is the lack of standardized testing conditions, which hinders cross-study comparison. A two-tier assessment and reporting logic is therefore proposed to distinguish degradation under defined nominal conditions from recovery and resilience following operational disturbances. Looking forward, two research directions merit priority: standardized stability assessment and the development of functionally resilient systems that can manage and recover from performance loss. Prioritizing stability from the earliest stages of material design is essential to bridge the gap between laboratory-scale promise and real-world water treatment deployment.

Water Research.title: Zero-valent iron enhanced simultaneous anammox-denitrification (SAD) for livestock wastewater treatment: dose-dependent responses and potential mass-transfer constraints induced by Fe-P mineralization.
Water Research.abstract: Zero-valent iron (ZVI) is capable of boosting simultaneous anammox and denitrification (SAD), yet the dose-dependent trade-off between nutrient removal and sludge interfacial properties, especially Fe-P mineralization-induced mass-transfer limitation, remains poorly understood. In this study, four continuous-flow upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactors with ZVI dosages of 0, 4, 8, and 12 g·L-1 were operated to evaluate nitrogen and phosphorus removal from simulated livestock anaerobic digestate. A dose-dependent trade-off was observed between moderate biological stimulation by ZVI and performance deterioration induced by excessive iron loading. Among the tested dosages, 4 g·L-1 ZVI yielded the optimal performance, with steady-state dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and COD removal efficiencies of 96.50% and 93.08%, respectively; the stoichiometrically estimated anammox contribution to DIN removal was 86.10%. Under this condition, the anammox-associated genera Candidatus Kuenenia and Candidatus Brocadia (combined relative abundance: 10.50%) coexisted with Pseudomonas (6.80%), a genus containing potentially denitrifying members, alongside favorable DIN removal. Increasing ZVI dosage further promoted phosphorus sequestration but failed to improve overall DIN removal. At 12 g·L-1, NH4⁺-N removal dropped below 15%, indicating severe deterioration of nitrogen removal capacity under excessive ZVI loading. Material characterization revealed that excess Fe2+ released from ZVI corrosion reacted with phosphate to form Fe-P mineral encrustation on granular sludge surfaces, accompanied by enhanced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) deposition. The formed mineralized layer increased interfacial mass-transfer resistance, hindering substrate diffusion into the inner active zones of granules and driving microbial succession toward iron-tolerant denitrifiers, thereby suppressing anammox activity. Collectively, 4 g·L-1 was identified as the optimal ZVI dosage within the tested range, achieving a favorable balance among DIN removal, phosphorus sequestration, and microbial community structure. These findings suggest that excessive Fe-P mineralization may constrain substrate accessibility in ZVI-amended granular SAD systems.

Water Research.title: Flood and low-flow dynamics across tile-drainage gradients in Midwestern U.S. watersheds.
Water Research.abstract: Subsurface tile drainage alters water movement through agricultural landscapes, potentially affecting watershed responses to both excess water and water scarcity. However, how flood and low-flow characteristics vary across watersheds with different tile-drainage percentages remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to evaluate its broader hydrological implications. We examined flood and low-flow events during 1981-2023 across approximately 500 non-nested Midwestern watersheds spanning tile-drainage percentages from 0% to over 80%. Annual discharge deviation was defined as the percentage difference between annual mean discharge and each watershed's long-term mean discharge. Watersheds with higher tile-drainage percentages generally exhibited larger positive deviations during wet years (precipitation anomaly >1σ) and more negative deviations during dry years (precipitation anomaly <-1σ). Positive discharge deviations during wet years were generally greater in magnitude than negative deviations during dry years, although these patterns varied seasonally. At the event scale, tile-drainage percentage was positively associated with flood runoff volume and low-flow deficit and negatively associated with flood-low-flow transition frequency. Analyses using tile-drainage percentage as the sole predictor revealed nonlinear relationships, including relatively elevated peak discharge at intermediate drainage percentages. After accounting for precipitation, topography, soil texture, and cropland coverage, associations with flood runoff, peak discharge, low-flow deficit, and low-flow duration remained statistically significant, although the flood-runoff and peak-discharge relationships became approximately linear. These findings show that hydrological characteristics vary systematically across the tile-drainage gradient, while also indicating that some apparent relationships are partly associated with differences in climate and landscape characteristics among watersheds. Our results highlight the importance of considering both flood and low-flow responses, together with climatic and landscape conditions, when evaluating tile-drainage design and watershed management.

Water Research.title: EPS-mediated metal retention extends bacterial protection across species during manure compost recycling.
Water Research.abstract: Bacterial detoxification traits can protect individual cells from heavy metals, but whether these benefits extend to neighboring species and ultimately influence metal fate remains unclear. We investigated this across four manure composting systems using community profiling, isolate-level EPS perturbations, co-cultures, and bioaugmentation. Correlation and Random Forest analyses linked substrate-specific bacterial taxa to operationally stable Cu/Zn fractions. Pig-compost-derived isolates affiliated with these taxa exhibited higher EPS production and predominantly surface-associated Cu/Zn retention. Alginate deletion reduced Cu and Zn surface adsorption by 47% and 25%, respectively, while increasing intracellular accumulation by ∼30%; D-tyrosine treatment and surface EPS stripping showed similar metal-partitioning responses, with exopolysaccharides most strongly associated with surface retention. In co-cultures, wild-type C1 increased the growth of comparison partners to an average of 1.9 times their monoculture levels, whereas alginate deletion weakened this benefit. C1-derived EPS preparations also promoted partner growth more effectively than equivalent-carbon cell-free supernatants. Bioaugmentation with the high-EPS consortium reduced soil-available Cu/Zn and maize leaf Cu/Zn concentrations by averages of 47.7% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to uninoculated controls. Together, these findings link polysaccharide-associated extracellular Cu/Zn retention to interspecies facilitation and highlight its potential for trait-guided metal stabilization during manure compost recycling.

mSphere.title: mSphere Legacy: Musings on a life exploring microbes.
mSphere.abstract: Through the lens of a third person narrative, the author describes his life history in the microbial sciences, prescribes by way of suggesting, and offers reasons to remain optimistic.

mSphere.title: pH-based inactivation of highly pathogenic H5N1 virus in unpasteurized milk.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 was confirmed in dairy cattle in March 2024 and subsequently spread to dairy herds throughout the United States, resulting in spillover cases in humans and other animals. Milk produced by infected dairy cattle, which has been shown to harbor high viral titers, poses a potential threat to peridomestic wildlife around dairies due to lack of treatment and disposal in wastewater systems that are often open to the environment. Here, we investigated a method for inactivating H5N1 virus in unpasteurized milk, utilizing the irreversible conformational change of the hemagglutinin (HA) glycoprotein induced by low pH. The pH needed for complete inactivation of three distinct influenza A viruses was determined for subsequent use in acidifying milk. The use of common, readily available acidification solutions like vinegar demonstrated that a 3% final concentration of vinegar (pH 3.6) induced complete inactivation of H5N1 in unpasteurized milk after 60 min. Our results suggest that pH-based inactivation of H5N1 in unpasteurized milk is a quick, feasible strategy that could be used on dairy farms prior to disposal of contaminated milk, thus reducing the risks of environmental contamination and exposure of animals around farms. [IMPORTANCE] Dairy farms experiencing outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 generate large volumes of milk with high titers of infectious H5N1 virus. While milk from sick cows does not enter the consumer supply chain, disposal of this untreated, contaminated milk through on-site wastewater systems still poses a significant risk for environmental contamination and exposure of peridomestic wildlife, potentially leading to spillover events. A simple method for inactivation of virus in milk prior to disposal could mitigate this risk. We show that lowering the pH of virus-laden milk with commercially available vinegar can neutralize dairy cattle H5N1 virus within 1 h, providing a quick and effective strategy for potential use on dairies to inactivate the virus in milk before disposal.

mSphere.title: Microbiota modulation impacts life history traits and mating success in male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit multiple arboviruses, but population suppression through the mass release of sterile or incompatible male mosquitoes can effectively reduce populations. These methods depend on the reliable mass-rearing of healthy, robust males that can successfully mate with wild females. The microbiota is a critical component of the larval diet, and its modulation can dramatically influence life history traits relevant to mass-rearing and male quality. Here, we used axenic (microbe-free), monoxenic (inoculated with Escherichia coli), and "laboratory community" mosquitoes (inoculated with an undefined microbiota derived from laboratory mosquitoes) to show that longevity was significantly enhanced in axenic and monoxenic males compared to laboratory community males. Moreover, monoxenic males more efficiently obtained mates in non-competitive mating scenarios compared to laboratory community males. However, microbiota treatment had no effect on mating success when males from different treatments competed for a mate. Our findings suggest that the microbiota is a key determinant of male mosquito life history, with direct implications for optimizing production of males for control programs. [IMPORTANCE] The microbes found in association with mosquitoes are crucial to mosquito development and have the capacity to influence multiple life history traits. In the current study, we comprehensively and functionally evaluate the role of the microbiota in mating success and other life history traits of male mosquitoes. Males are crucial to disease transmission, via their role in mating, and via their use in mosquito population control. By focusing on males, the understudied sex in mosquito research, we provide novel and foundational insight into how microbial communities influence male life history traits and mating success. Moreover, our findings establish a critical framework for understanding how the microbiota may affect male quality, production efficiency, and performance in vector control programs that involve mass production of adult male mosquitoes.

mSphere.title: Bridging generalizability and reproducibility in machine learning-based antimicrobial resistance prediction.
mSphere.abstract: The rapid growth of whole-genome sequencing and machine learning (ML) has led to a multitude of methods for predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from bacterial genomic data. Despite increasingly high reported predictive performance, substantial differences in data sets, phenotype definitions, genomic preprocessing, evaluation strategies, and validation procedures make it difficult to determine whether models will perform reliably beyond the data on which they were developed. In machine learning, this problem is generally framed in terms of generalizability: the ability of a model to maintain performance when applied to previously unseen data. In microbiology, many of the same considerations ultimately manifest as a problem of reproducibility. In this review, we provide a brief overview of the fundamental concepts underlying machine learning-based AMR prediction and then examine the factors that affect model generalizability and reproducibility.

mSphere.title: A highly conserved two-gene operon is crucial for lipoarabinomannan localization, pathogenesis, and cell envelope function in Mycobacterium abscessus.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Mycobacterium abscessus is an emerging threat, causing infections that are difficult to treat due to intrinsic resistance to most antibiotics. Determinants of M. abscessus physiology and pathogenesis remain poorly understood, hampering therapeutic development. Here, we show that in M. abscessus, the lprg-mfs operon is essential for virulence in macrophages and mice. Loss of lprg-mfs in M. abscessus causes accumulation of the glycolipid lipoarabinomannan (LAM) on the cell surface and in culture supernatant, suggesting that this system participates in LAM import. This contrasts with its proposed role in M. tuberculosis, where lprg-mfs has been implicated in the export of various lipids. Consistent with altered lipid distribution, the lprg-mfs mutant displays severe defects in mycomembrane permeability, fluidity, and integrity, and expression of mfs alone restores only a subset of these phenotypes, revealing a surprising uncoupling of envelope fluidity and permeability. Using a suppressor screen to further investigate the factors that control the distribution of lipoarabinomannan, we find that a point mutation in the unannotated gene MAB_0995 can fully or partially rescue all deletion mutant phenotypes. Our data also show that lipoarabinomannan in the mycomembrane is dynamically regulated in response to environmental conditions, including hypoxia and macrophage infection. Together, these findings redefine the role of LprG and Mfs in mycobacterial cell envelope homeostasis and reveal unexpected plasticity in mycomembrane lipid regulation in M. abscessus. [IMPORTANCE] The emerging pathogen Mycobacterium abscessus causes life-threatening lung infections in certain patients that are extremely difficult to treat due to its intrinsic resistance to most antibiotics. However, the process by which this organism establishes infection is poorly understood, as are the specific determinants of antibiotic tolerance. Better knowledge of the genes required for virulence and impermeability to antibiotics in M. abscessus could enable the development of more effective treatments. The significance of this study is the demonstration that the lprg-mfs operon is required for both pathogenesis and impermeability in M. abscessus. Furthermore, our study shows a correlation between cell envelope characteristics and the distribution of the molecule lipoarabinomannan, suggesting a specific mechanism by which these crucial characteristics are mediated.

mSphere.title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131.
mSphere.abstract: Escherichia coli ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics of E. coli ST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the key kpsM and kpsT genes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR) Escherichia coli is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone of E. coli that is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.

mSphere.title: Two Ume6 target gene classes in the biofilm regulatory network of Candida albicans.
mSphere.abstract: Biofilm formation by the fungal pathogen Candida albicans is a major source of infection. The biofilm regulator Ume6 forms complexes with partner transcription factors Efg1, Ndt80, and Upc2 to drive expression of biofilm-related genes. Here, we present chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing data for Ume6-chromatin association in both wild-type and efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ upc2Δ/Δ backgrounds. Ume6 associates with two promoter region classes. For one class, Ume6 association is significantly decreased in the efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ upc2Δ/Δ background. This class includes 577 genes, many with well-established roles in biofilm formation or the related process of filamentation. For the second class, Ume6 association is unperturbed in the triple mutant background. This class includes 534 genes, some with roles in iron homeostasis (e.g., SFU1) and ergosterol synthesis (e.g., ERG11), which may contribute to the impact of Ume6 on ndt80Δ/Δ mutant azole drug sensitivity. It also includes FLO9, a putative adhesin gene that is required for the emergent biofilm state produced by efg1Δ/Δ ndt80Δ/Δ double mutants. The data show that Ume6 binding to about half of its targets requires known partners, and Ume6 binding to about half of its targets does not. Ume6 may bind to the latter set of promoter regions independently of any partner, or perhaps with additional partners that have yet to be discovered.IMPORTANCEBiofilm formation has a central role in infection by the fungal pathogen Candida albicans. Here, we focus on a key regulator, Ume6, that can drive biofilm formation. It is known to form protein complexes with three partner transcription factors, and here, we investigate Ume6-promoter binding in the presence and absence of those partners. Ume6 binds to two promoter classes: one depends on known partners, and many associated genes have roles in biofilm formation. The second class is independent of known partners, and some associated genes are functionally connected to iron metabolism and ergosterol synthesis. The second class may mediate effects of Ume6 on azole drug sensitivity. Our results suggest that Ume6 may bind to some promoter regions independently of any partner, or perhaps with additional partners that have yet to be discovered.

mSphere.title: Oya virus reporter systems for high-throughput screening of viral replication inhibitors in mosquito cells.
mSphere.abstract: Orthobunyaviruses are a diverse group of arboviruses, yet reporter virus-based inhibitor screening in mosquito-derived cells remains underexplored. Oya virus (OYAV), a Simbu serogroup orthobunyavirus detected in humans, mosquitoes, and midges, currently lacks reverse genetics tools and quantitative compound screening platforms. In this study, we established the first plasmid-based reverse genetics system for OYAV, successfully rescuing recombinant wild-type virus (rOYAV/WT) alongside fluorescent reporter viruses expressing enhanced green fluorescent protein (rOYAV/eGFP/S) or mCherry (rOYAV/mCherry/S). Both reporter viruses maintained stable reporter expression and infectivity across multiple vertebrate and mosquito-derived cell lines, although reporter insertion resulted in attenuated replication compared with the parental virus. Leveraging the robust fluorescence signal and retention of the reporter-containing region during serial passage, we developed a mosquito cell-based high-content screening platform to identify compounds inhibiting OYAV replication in C6/36 cells. The assay demonstrated high robustness and reproducibility, with a Z' factor of 0.755, and showed strong correlation with wild-type virus replication profiles. By screening an 800-compound library, we identified 10 candidates exhibiting >95% inhibitory activity against OYAV replication. Among these, saikosaponin B2, fingolimod (hydrochloride), and fangchinoline displayed micromolar inhibitory effects against both reporter and wild-type OYAV replication, with limited cytotoxicity in C6/36 cells. Collectively, this study establishes the reverse genetics system for OYAV and a quantitative mosquito-cell-based screening platform for orthobunyavirus replication inhibitors, providing a valuable tool for studying OYAV replication and evaluating antiviral compounds in mosquito-derived cells.IMPORTANCEOya virus (OYAV) is an emerging arbovirus circulating in Asia, with documented infection in humans and arthropod vectors. However, the absence of reverse genetics and reporter systems has limited mechanistic studies and inhibitor discovery for OYAV, particularly in arthropod-derived cells. Here, we established a reverse genetics system and generated fluorescent reporter viruses that enable real-time monitoring of OYAV replication. The optimized reporter virus was further used to establish a high-throughput inhibitor screening platform in mosquito C6/36 cells, leading to the identification of three compounds with inhibitory activity and low cytotoxicity in this system. These tools provide a foundation for investigating OYAV biology and facilitate the discovery and evaluation of inhibitors in vector cells and potentially in live vectors.

mSphere.title: LPC(16:0) and prothrombin time as mortality predictors in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome.
mSphere.abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne viral disease with a high fatality rate. However, the impact of the SFTS virus (SFTSV) on host lipid metabolism and its relationship with the prognosis of patients remain unclear. To determine the lipid metabolism profile of SFTSV-infected and identify prognostic biomarkers, targeted lipidomics analysis was conducted on SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and serum samples from 71 subjects (including 15 healthy controls, 35 SFTS survivors, and 21 SFTS deceased patients) in this study. Our findings revealed that glycerophospholipid metabolism was the most significantly disrupted pathway in both SFTSV-infected Huh7 cells and SFTS patients, with lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) species, including LPC(16:1), LPC(18:1), LPC(16:0), and LPC(18:0), showing decreased levels. Together with clinical parameters, prothrombin time (PT) and LPC(16:0) were further identified as prognostic factors, and the combined model incorporating these two markers predicted mortality with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.937. These findings provide a foundation for mortality prediction and mechanistic understanding of SFTS.IMPORTANCEEffective prognostic tools and targeted therapies for SFTS remain urgently needed, as current clinical management relies largely on supportive care and lacks reliable indicators for early risk stratification. This study enhances our understanding of lipid alterations following SFTSV infection, opens potential avenues for metabolism-targeted intervention, and may aid in assessing disease progression and guiding appropriate clinical interventions.

mSphere.title: SARS-CoV-2 membrane (M) protein activates TLR4 to induce an inflammatory response.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] An excessive inflammatory response, also known as "cytokine storm," is a major cause of severe COVID-19. Viral RNA and its structural proteins are key mediators of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation. While the immune sensors and host inflammatory responses induced by SARS-CoV-2 RNA and the structural proteins spike (S), envelope (E), and nucleocapsid (N) are well defined, the role of membrane (M) protein in inflammatory/antiviral response and the signaling pathway facilitating M protein-mediated immune response is not well characterized. Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 M protein induces robust inflammatory cytokine responses in murine and human macrophages and lungs. We also show that the M protein-induced inflammatory response relies on TLR4 signaling and that MyD88 serves as the key adaptor driving inflammation, while TRIF is primarily required for the antiviral IFN response. Detailed evaluation of downstream signaling pathways highlighted the critical roles of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) molecules JNK and ERK1/2, followed by nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and p38 signaling in the M protein-TLR4-mediated inflammatory response. Finally, we show that abrogation of M protein-induced ERK1/2 and p38 signaling reduced inflammatory cytokine production and rescued type I interferon production in wild-type macrophages, while inhibition of JNK and NF-κB suppressed the M protein-induced inflammatory and antiviral cytokine responses. Collectively, our results demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 M protein induces pro-inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons via TLR4-MyD88/TRIF activation, with MAPK activation playing a dominant role, and offer specific targeting of MAPK signaling to mitigate SARS-CoV-2-induced excessive inflammation and pathology. [IMPORTANCE] Severe COVID-19 is often caused by an excessive inflammatory response, but the role of the SARS-CoV-2 membrane (M) protein in this process has not been well understood. We show that the M protein strongly activates inflammatory and antiviral immune responses through TLR4 signaling and identify the key signaling pathways involved. We also demonstrate that selectively targeting MAPK signaling can reduce harmful inflammation while restoring antiviral interferon responses. These findings improve our understanding of how SARS-CoV-2 causes disease and identify potential therapeutic targets to limit excessive inflammation without compromising antiviral immunity.

mSphere.title: Identification of a novel equine rotavirus B from Missouri in 2025, which is distantly related to group B rotaviruses.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Despite the wide circulation of group B rotaviruses in animals and humans, rotavirus B was not found in horses until 2021 in Kentucky, USA. Little is known about the genetic diversity and evolution of rotavirus B in this new host. Here, we described a divergent equine rotavirus B (ERVB) from a foal with idiopathic diarrhea in Missouri (designated MO-ERVB-25). Full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that MO-ERVB-25 is distantly related to all previously known group B rotaviruses, including ERVB strains identified in 2021 in Kentucky (KY-ERVB-21). The mean nucleotide substitution rate of the VP4 segment was estimated as 1.44 × 10-3 substitutions/site/year, which is a magnitude higher than the VP7 segment. We further demonstrated that MO-ERVB-25, like human RVB, binds chemically neutral LacNAc-containing complex N-linked glycans, while KY-ERVB-21 recognizes negatively charged polysialic acid (polySia) with α-2,8-linkage, which is a functional receptor for unrelated enteric human adenovirus 52. Using the AlphaFold-enabled structure prediction, we showed that both MO-ERVB-25 and human RVB VP8* lack a novel C-terminal α2 helix that is only observed in the KY-ERVB-21 VP8*, which may help explain the difference in glycan binding specificities. Finally, screening of foal samples by the reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay identified 4.2% of idiopathic foal diarrhea samples (6 out of 140) positive for MO-ERVB-25. These results suggest that MO-ERVB-25 represents a new rotavirus B subgroup that circulates in foals. Its circulation, together with KY-ERVB-25 subgroup, raises the possibility of reassortment and antigenic shift as mechanisms of rotavirus B evolution in equines. [IMPORTANCE] Equine RVB (ERVB) has emerged as a significant cause of foal diarrhea since 2021. Our study describes a highly divergent RVB strain identified in a foal with severe diarrhea in 2025. This ERVB variant exhibited low amino acid identity compared with previously reported ERVB strains. The novel ERVB strain escaped routine diagnostic detection. Sequence analysis demonstrated that this new strain grouped with bovine, porcine, caprine, and equine RVB but formed a distinct, independent branch. In addition, glycan array studies revealed the substantial difference in glycan recognition between new and previously described ERVB strains, which is likely determined by the presence or absence of a novel C-terminal α2 helix in the VP8* receptor-binding domain. These results suggest that this novel ERVB variant may co-circulate with existing ERVB strains in horses, which may facilitate rapid viral evolution through antigenic diversity, a property previously reported in rotaviruses from other hosts.

mSphere.title: Phage-encoded PciP differentially regulates Pseudomonas aeruginosa swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms.
mSphere.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen whose intrinsic antibiotic resistance and complex virulence regulatory networks pose major clinical challenges. Bacteriophages and their encoded proteins have emerged as potential modulators of bacterial physiology, yet the mechanisms by which phage proteins influence bacterial virulence remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified PciP, an early protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, which suppresses pyocyanin production and swarming motility in P. aeruginosa. PciP reduces PQS levels and suppresses quorum-sensing gene transcription. PciP associates with CheV, and genetic analysis indicates that CheV is required for the PciP-mediated inhibition of swarming but not for the PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production. Expression of PciP attenuates virulence in infection models. Together, these findings reveal that PciP differentially modulates swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms. These results provide mechanistic insights into how a phage-encoded protein reprograms host regulatory networks.IMPORTANCEPseudomonas aeruginosa is a major opportunistic pathogen that is increasingly difficult to treat due to intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance. Bacteriophages encode diverse proteins that can interfere with bacterial regulatory networks, yet many remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we characterize PciP, a protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, and show that it modulates bacterial motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes through distinct mechanisms. PciP associates with CheV and inhibits swarming motility in a CheV-dependent manner, whereas PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production persists in the absence of CheV. These combined effects significantly reduce pathogenicity in both animal and plant infection models. This study advances our understanding of phage-host interactions by demonstrating that a phage-encoded protein can differentially modulate host regulatory outputs via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms.

mSphere.title: Natural variation of hypervirulent Klebsiella pathogenicity loci among Taiwan bloodstream isolates.
mSphere.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of both nosocomial and community-acquired infections, with hypervirulent (hvKP) strains causing severe disease in healthy individuals. In Southeastern Asia, diabetes mellitus is a recognized risk factor for hvKP-associated pyogenic liver abscesses. hvKP virulence is typically attributed to carriage of a large virulence plasmid encoding siderophore biosynthesis (iuc, iro) and mucoid regulator (rmpA, rmpA2) genes. Here, we analyzed 50 bloodstream isolates from Taipei, Taiwan, to investigate genomic and phenotypic characteristics of isolates from patients with or without diabetes mellitus. In diabetic patients and patients with liver abscesses, hvKP biomarkers were found in 66% (n = 33) and 64% (n = 32) of isolates, respectively. While we expected hvKP isolates to be overrepresented in this collection, we observed extensive diversity among hvKP pathogenicity loci, with strains of typical ST23 hvKP lineages carrying incomplete KpVP-1 virulence plasmids. This hvKP biomarker diversity is typically found in classical multidrug-resistant lineages that have acquired portions of the virulence plasmid. Phenotypic assays showed that hvKP biomarkers did not strictly predict hypermucoviscosity, capsule and siderophore production, or survival in serum. Loss of rmpA consistently eliminated hypermucoviscosity and reduced virulence in a murine pneumonia model, whereas aerobactin loss did not. In vivo studies demonstrated variations in virulence that could not be explained solely by differences in the number of hypervirulence-associated loci. These findings highlight the complexity of K. pneumoniae pathogenesis and demonstrate that while canonical biomarkers effectively distinguish hvKP from classical K. pneumoniae, they are insufficient to predict variation in virulence among hvKP strains. Our findings provide insight into the virulence spectrum of strains carrying incomplete plasmid configurations.IMPORTANCEK. pneumoniae poses a global health threat due to the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. We identified substantial diversity in virulence plasmid content, including incomplete virulence plasmids within archetypal hvKP lineages, and showed that phenotypic and in vivo virulence traits cannot be fully explained by the presence or absence of individual hypervirulence-associated loci. While canonical biomarkers such as rmpA and iuc are widely used to distinguish hypervirulent strains, our analysis demonstrates that no single biomarker is sufficient to reliably predict pathogenic potential and that virulence depends on specific locus combinations and broader context. These findings highlight a critical gap in our understanding of hvKP pathogenesis, underscoring the need for more nuanced frameworks to evaluate virulence. This work has important implications for clinical diagnostics, surveillance, and risk assessment of emerging K. pneumoniae strains worldwide.

mSphere.title: A novel technique to characterize Klebsiella pneumoniae populations indicates that mono-colonization is associated with risk of infection.
mSphere.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae and related species are a common cause of healthcare-associated infections. The gut is a major Klebsiella reservoir, and gut colonization is a risk factor for developing an extraintestinal Klebsiella infection. Patients can be colonized by multiple Klebsiella strains or even species in the gut simultaneously, and there is high concordance between the gut-colonizing and infection-causing strains. The detection and characterization of colonizing strains is critical for a better understanding of the progression to infection and for developing interventions for colonized patients. However, the association between mixed or mono-colonization and subsequent infection is unknown. In this study, we developed an amplicon-based sequencing method called wzi-Seq that enables the detection and quantification of Klebsiella strains from complex samples and mixtures using the conserved capsule gene wzi as a molecular barcode. This method is highly accurate and precise, with a sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 99.8% in mixtures containing as many as 58 unique wzi types, and 90.8% concordance with culture-based detection from archived rectal swab samples from an established case and control cohort. Adjudicating wzi-Seq with culture data, we determined that 63.2% (108/171) patients were mono-colonized with a single Klebsiella strain, while 36.8% (63/171) had mixed colonization with multiple Klebsiella strains. Controlling for patient variables in multivariate analysis, we determined that mono-colonization was significantly (P = 0.034) associated with infection. Characterization of Klebsiella colonizing populations could improve the accuracy of assessing infection risk and enable targeted interventions to prevent these healthcare-associated infections.IMPORTANCEKlebsiella gut colonization is a major risk factor for the development of extraintestinal Klebsiella infections in hospitalized settings. However, it is unknown if patients are colonized by one or multiple strains of Klebsiella and how the population structure of Klebsiella in the gut impacts infection risk. Here, we describe the development of a novel technique, wzi-Seq, to detect and quantify multiple Klebsiella strains from complex samples using standard techniques and rapid DNA sequencing. We applied wzi-Seq to rectal swabs from a well-characterized patient cohort and found that Klebsiella colonization with a single strain was more prevalent than colonization with multiple strains. Furthermore, mono-colonized patients had a significantly higher risk of developing a Klebsiella infection than mixed-colonized patients. This work validates a new tool to study Klebsiella populations and reveals that population structure in the gut influences the risk of healthcare-associated infections.

mSphere.title: NEK kinase TcRDK2 controls differentiation, host cell infection, and remodeling of the translation initiation machinery in Trypanosoma cruzi.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Trypanosoma cruzi, the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, alternates between replicative epimastigotes and amastigotes and non-dividing, mammal-infective metacyclic and bloodstream trypomastigotes. Protein phosphorylation is a major regulatory mechanism in trypanosomatids, whose kinomes reveal an expanded family of NIMA-related kinases (NEKs). Here, we investigated the role of T. cruzi RDK2 (repressor of differentiation kinase 2), a conserved NEK that carries a C-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. Endogenous gene tagging showed that TcRDK2 is expressed in all major life cycle stages and displays a cytoplasmic distribution. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TcRDK2 did not markedly alter epimastigote growth in rich medium but caused a significant accumulation of cells with abnormal nucleus/kinetoplast configurations, consistent with defects in kinetoplast segregation and cytokinesis; TcRDK2-null parasites also showed reduced in vitro metacyclogenesis and failed to establish efficient infections in human fibroblasts. To probe gain-of-function effects, we generated tetracycline-inducible overexpression lines for full-length TcRDK2 (RDK2WT), a PH-deleted variant (RDK2ΔPH), and a catalytically dead mutant (RDK2K70A). Overexpression of RDK2WT or RDK2ΔPH decreased epimastigote growth, enhanced metacyclogenesis, and strongly impaired host cell invasion and intracellular amastigote proliferation, with more pronounced phenotypes for RDK2ΔPH, suggesting that the PH domain normally restrains TcRDK2 activity in vivo. Phosphoproteomic profiling of RDK2WT-overexpressing epimastigotes revealed broad phosphoproteome remodeling associated with TcRDK2 upregulation, including changes affecting proteins linked to translation initiation and the cytoskeleton. Together, these findings support a role for TcRDK2 as a NEK kinase in kinetoplast replication/segregation, metacyclogenesis, and host cell infection in T. cruzi and highlight TcRDK2 as a promising kinetoplastid-specific therapeutic target for Chagas disease. [IMPORTANCE] Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major health problem with limited treatment options. To persist in both insect vectors and mammalian hosts, the parasite must precisely coordinate cell division, differentiation into infectious forms, and survival inside host cells. Protein kinases are central regulators of these processes and attractive drug targets, yet many remain poorly understood in T. cruzi. In this study, we investigate RDK2, a member of the NIMA-related kinase family. Using gene knockout, inducible overexpression, and global analysis of phosphorylated proteins, we show that RDK2 is required for accurate segregation of mitochondrial DNA, efficient formation of infective insect stage forms, and successful infection and replication in human cells. These findings identify RDK2 as a key regulator that links parasite cell division to infectivity and highlight it as a promising, parasite-specific candidate for future drug development against Chagas disease.

mSphere.title: Temporal regulation of metabolic processes in the marine diazotroph Crocosphaera watsonii WH8501.
mSphere.abstract: Marine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play a crucial role in oceanic nitrogen cycling, supporting primary production and ecosystem balance. Crocosphaera watsonii WH8501 exemplifies this capability by temporally separating photosynthesis and diazotrophy. To investigate the regulatory mechanisms underlying this process, we employed mass spectrometry-based proteomics in a high-resolution diel culturing experiment, revealing tightly coordinated protein abundance patterns. Unsupervised clustering of diel protein abundance profiles identified six groups of co-regulated proteins characterized by distinct temporal expression patterns and functional categories. Cluster 1 contained nitrogen fixation and amino acid biosynthesis proteins that peaked at night, while cluster 2 included glycogen metabolism and photosynthetic dark reaction proteins that were most abundant during the night and day-night transition, supporting carbon consumption and energy production. Clusters 3 and 4 were enriched in proteins involved in photosynthesis, cell division, and lipid synthesis, with maximal abundance around midday. Cluster 5 comprised peptide biosynthesis proteins that peaked later in the day and may facilitate nitrogenase complex formation. Cluster 6, expressed during the day-night transition, revealed coordinated nitrogenase assembly, with Fe-S cluster proteins preceding peak nitrogenase iron protein abundance, suggesting a temporally ordered sequence of enzyme maturation. Distinct temporal patterns in iron trafficking to heme and Fe-S cluster biosynthetic systems further indicated tightly regulated allocation of iron to metalloproteins across the diel cycle. Together, these results reveal the intricate temporal coordination that enables Crocosphaera to balance nitrogen fixation and photosynthesis within a single cell and underscore the central role of diel regulation in sustaining these globally important processes.IMPORTANCEMarine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play an essential role in global nitrogen cycling and ocean productivity. In this study, we investigate the temporal regulation of Crocosphaera watsonii metabolism using high-resolution proteomics under diel culturing conditions. Our analysis resolves six distinct clusters of protein abundance patterns across the light/dark cycle, reflecting intricate coordination of nitrogen fixation, photosynthesis, carbon allocation, and iron homeostasis. Notably, we identify temporally ordered assembly of nitrogenase subunits, including precursory expression of Fe-S cluster proteins and indications of tightly controlled iron trafficking systems. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into how unicellular diazotrophs synchronize key metabolic processes under natural diel cycles.

mSphere.title: Extracellular vesicles released by Candida albicans yeast cells impact candidiasis lethality in insect and murine models.
mSphere.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are nano-sized lipid bilayer structures released by diverse cell types. For pathogenic fungi, EVs play critical roles by modulating immune responses and influencing disease progression. Previously, we demonstrated that vaccination with EVs from Candida albicans promoted protection in immunosuppressed mice subsequently infected with lethal doses of this organism. However, the impact of EVs in the presence of fungi is poorly investigated in vivo. Here, we demonstrated that co-injection of C. albicans yeasts and their EVs into Galleria mellonella larvae led to a rapid larval death compared to yeast cells alone. This effect seems to be associated with thermosensitive compounds, such as secreted aspartic proteases (Saps), virulence factors carried by C. albicans EVs. EVs from SAP knockout (KO) strains (sap1/2/3Δ and sap9Δ) impaired this harmful effect, confirming the crucial role of Saps. Deletion of SAP1-3 prevented the EV-associated decrease in hemocyte density, whereas SAP9 deletion impaired the increase in oxidative response and melanin production. In a murine model of disseminated candidiasis with intraperitoneal infection, the deleterious effect of C. albicans EVs was observed only when co-injected intraperitoneally with yeasts, but not when EVs were administered intramuscularly. Therefore, both fungal cells and EVs are required for the pathogenic effects. Our findings confirm the aggressive role of fungal EVs in the presence of C. albicans and reinforce their contribution to candidiasis, elucidating EV-pathogen interactions. Although these results do not preclude the use of C. albicans EVs in vaccine formulations, they emphasize the need to consider delivery route and presence of virulence factors.IMPORTANCEFungal infections caused by Candida albicans represent a significant threat, particularly to immunocompromised individuals. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) from fungi have been explored as promising vaccine formulations, with demonstrated protective effects. However, previous studies have also suggested that EVs may contribute to disease progression. Here, we demonstrate that EVs enhance fungal pathogenicity in vivo and identify key factors driving this effect. We show that EV-associated aspartyl proteases (secreted aspartic proteases [Saps]), along with other virulence components, directly contribute to accelerated host mortality when EVs are present alongside fungal cells, and that this outcome depends on both their composition and route of delivery. By demonstrating the involvement of EV-associated Saps in disease progression, this work advances our understanding of host-pathogen interactions and reveals critical considerations for the safe development of EV-based therapeutic and vaccine strategies.

mSphere.title: Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism.
mSphere.abstract: Pediatric infections with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden in vivo, and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp in vitro. Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae are responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae in children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition on K. pneumoniae colonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of K. pneumoniae. Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae.

mSphere.title: Characterization of the Peromyscus leucopus immunoglobulin germline repertoire and anti-OspA antibody response reveals conserved germline IGHV features among cricetid rodents.
mSphere.abstract: Peromyscus leucopus (P. leucopus) is an important reservoir host for several zoonoses, including Borrelia burgdorferi (B. burgdorferi), the causative agent of Lyme disease. However, the immunoglobulin germline repertoire underlying antibody responses in this reservoir host remains poorly defined. In this study, we characterized the immunoglobulin variable genes of P. leucopus and identified 12 IGHV, 12 IGKV, and 3 IGLV gene families comprising 129, 87, and 12 genes, respectively. These genes exhibited similar usage patterns to those of Mus musculus (M. musculus). We also identified a high-divergence region (HDR) within the germline IGHV loci of three Borrelia sp.-susceptible Cricetidae species, P. leucopus, Peromyscus maniculatus (P. maniculatus), and Arvicola amphibius (A. amphibius). Compared with the corresponding regions in Muridae species, the Cricetidae HDRs are expanded and contain a large number of IGHV genes. To investigate the antigen-specific features of the repertoire, we analyzed the antibody responses of P. leucopus to B. burgdorferi outer surface protein A (OspA), a highly immunogenic tick midgut adhesin involved in midgut colonization. Comparative analysis of more than 140 IGHV genes from immunized P. leucopus showed that germline IGHV genes encoding anti-OspA antibodies exhibited higher sequence similarity to corresponding germline IGHV genes in P. maniculatus and A. amphibius than did P. leucopus germline IGHV genes not associated with anti-OspA responses.IMPORTANCEThis study characterized the immunoglobulin gene repertoire of Peromyscus leucopus and revealed extensive diversity across its variable-region loci. Analysis of antibody response to outer surface protein A (OspA) showed that germline IGHV genes encoding anti-OspA antibodies showed higher sequence similarity to their corresponding germline IGHV genes in other Borrelia-susceptible cricetid rodents, suggesting that conserved germline IGHV features are associated with OspA recognition. These findings lay the foundation for further understanding of antibody responses in this important reservoir host.

HIV-1 Tat protects macrophages from killing by the exoenzyme U from Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] People living with HIV (PLWH) have a higher risk of developing other diseases, such as bacterial pneumonia. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common cause of pneumonia in humans. The most virulent strains produce ExoU, which is a key effector of P. aeruginosa cytotoxicity. Upon injection into the target cell cytosol by the type III secretion system (T3SS), ExoU binds to PI(4,5)P2 on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. ExoU phospholipase activity then induces a loss of plasma membrane integrity, rapidly leading to cell death. HIV-1-Tat is secreted by HIV-infected cells, leading to nanomolar concentrations of Tat in the sera of PLWH, even under antiretroviral therapy. Circulating Tat is endocytosed by uninfected cells, translocates to the cytosol, and binds to PI(4,5)P2 at the plasma membrane. In uninfected cells only, Tat is palmitoylated, enabling Tat to become resident on PI(4,5)P2. Here, we found that Tat interferes with the recruitment of ExoU by PI(4,5)P2, thereby protecting primary human macrophages from the toxicity of exoU-positive P. aeruginosa strains. Tat nevertheless enhances the toxicity of exoU-deficient strains of P. aeruginosa toward macrophages. HIV Tat might, therefore, modulate the sensitivity of PLWH toward P. aeruginosa strains depending on whether they own the key type III effector exoU. [IMPORTANCE] Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common cause of pneumonia in humans and a major nosocomial pathogen. People living with HIV (PLWH), even under antiretroviral therapy, are at risk of developing infectious diseases, such as bacterial pneumonia. The T3SS plays an important role in P. aeruginosa virulence. The T3SS can inject four effectors into the target cell cytosol, including the key effector ExoU that binds to PI(4,5)P2 on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. The potent phospholipase activity of ExoU rapidly induces cell death. HIV-Tat is present in the serum of PLWH. Circulating Tat enters cells and binds PI(4,5)P2 with a very high affinity. Our results indicate that HIV-Tat interferes with the recruitment of ExoU by PI(4,5)P2, thereby protecting macrophages from strains of P. aeruginosa that express ExoU. Tat, nevertheless, increased macrophage sensitivity to exoU-negative strains. HIV Tat could, therefore, modulate PLWH susceptibility to P. aeruginosa.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Systematic benchmarking of Hi-C-based scaffolding methods in genome assembly
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractHigh-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) technology is crucial for scaffolding, a key step to generate chromosome-level high-quality genome assemblies. However, although several Hi-C-based scaffolding tools have been developed, their utility in genome assembly remains constrained by inconsistent performance, making a systematic benchmarking urgently needed. Here, we present a comprehensive benchmark of five prominent Hi-C scaffolders using simulated contig assemblies considering various factors, including contig lengths, chimeric contig proportions, Hi-C coverage depths, and ploidy levels. Our analysis revealed that chimeric contigs and species ploidy are the two factors with the greatest impact on scaffolding performance, making contig clustering the primary bottleneck. Additionally, we developed a novel metric termed the Hi-C scaffolding index to assess both scaffolding accuracy and genome assembly quality. We further demonstrated its utility in detecting assembly errors, thereby facilitating assembly quality improvements. Finally, evaluations across six real datasets revealed that current tools exhibit uniform reliability on diploid genomes but display marked performance disparities on polyploid genomes. Overall, our study provides a rigorous benchmark of current Hi-C scaffolding methods and offers actionable guidance for algorithm optimization and tool selection.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: MitoLODE: a virtual mitochondrion framework with knowledge graph priors for trajectory modeling and mechanistic perturbation analysis
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractMitochondria play a central role in the pathogenesis of major diseases. Tracking how they evolve under disease conditions is valuable for understanding pathological mechanisms and identifying intervention windows. Existing single-cell trajectory inference methods rely on pseudotime rather than a real temporal axis, and rarely model disease and control as independent trajectories. Virtual cell methods target one-shot drug perturbation responses and do not handle the continuous temporal evolution of disease phenotypes. To address these gaps, we propose a virtual mitochondrion research paradigm. We first curate and construct MitoKG, a mitochondria-specific heterogeneous knowledge graph integrated from five authoritative databases. MitoKG contains 2549 nodes of four types and 23 019 edges of five relation types. Building on these priors, we develop MitoLODE, a conditioned dual-trajectory neural ordinary differential equation framework. MitoLODE embeds graph priors and temporal features throughout encoding, continuous-time dynamics, and decoding, modeling disease and control evolution as two coupled paths. Benchmarked against eight baselines across four datasets covering Parkinson’s disease, cardiac, and pancreatic differentiation, MitoLODE leads in most settings and remains robust under low-data regimes and extrapolation to unseen time points. Two synthetic datasets with known ground truth validate its trajectory recovery under controlled conditions. Building on the trained model, we design a gradient-guided perturbation procedure that identifies potential intervention targets aligned with known Parkinson’s pathology. We develop MGMI, a large language model-based reasoning module that grounds model outputs in MitoKG nodes and turns them into confidence-graded mechanistic hypotheses, which nonetheless require experimental validation.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: DiffKnock: diffusion-based knockoff inference for neural networks with applications to single-cell RNA-sequencing data
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractHigh-throughput single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies have revolutionized our ability to characterize cellular heterogeneity and dissect gene regulatory mechanisms. These data, however, are inherently high-dimensional and correlated, posing substantial challenges for statistical inference and feature selection. Identifying disease-related genes, while rigorously controlling false discoveries, remains a key challenge in scRNA-seq data analysis. Traditional methods often rely on parametric assumptions, which may fail to capture complex relationships and can suffer from inflated false discovery rates (FDRs) in high-dimensional settings. We introduce DiffKnock, a diffusion-based knockoff framework for high-dimensional feature selection with finite-sample FDR control. DiffKnock addresses two key limitations of existing knockoff methods: preserving complex feature dependencies and detecting nonlinear associations. Our approach leverages diffusion models to generate valid knockoffs and employs neural network-based gradient and filter statistics to construct antisymmetric feature importance measures. Through simulations, DiffKnock demonstrates higher power than autoencoder-based, GAN-based, and Gaussian-based knockoff methods while maintaining target FDR, indicating superior performance in scenarios with complex nonlinear relationships. By applying the method to murine single-cell RNA-seq data of LPS-stimulated macrophages, we also identified canonical NF-$\kappa $B target genes (Ccl3, Hmox1). In another application to Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project donor-level pseudobulk transcriptomic data, DiffKnock further identifies a strong microglial signal for CERAD score, with PTPRG emerging as the most stable selected gene under both gradient- and filter-based statistics. These results highlight that, by combining flexible deep generative models with rigorous statistics, DiffKnock is a powerful and reliable tool for analyzing scRNA-seq data and other high-dimensional structured data.
